item.title: Hills and mountains
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
A girl’s story of forced marriage reveals how the Soviet invasion of 1979 transformed life in Afghanistan

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded: Directed by the Afghan-born Canadian filmmaker Salar Pashtoonyar, Hills and Mountains recalls how the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 upended life in the once-stable country. The story is told from the perspective of a woman whose identity Pashtoonyar has protected by using a voice actor and altering some details of her life. Born in 1969, she describes seeing the ‘peaceful and tolerant’ homeland of her childhood deteriorate into a place where parents married off their teenage daughters to keep them from starving. Ultimately, a false accusation of an affair led to her own forced marriage and shattered her family life. Pashtoonyar pairs her narration with sweeping scenes from the mountainous country, drawing out the intersections between landscape, lived experience and global history.

item.title: The physics of getting fired
item.dc:creator: Zahaan Bharmal
item.description:
Physics offered me a sense of order and purpose. But when life got messy I realised it had a much deeper insight to give

- by Zahaan Bharmal

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

21 minute listen

The senior partner didn’t waste any time. ‘I’m sorry, Zahaan,’ he said, ‘your services are no longer required at the firm.’ We sometimes called him the Burger King behind his back, because he ate a Whopper Meal at his desk every day. I’d never spoken to him before, and now I never would again.

It was the summer of 2001. I was fresh out of university and nine months into my first job as a management consultant in London. My parents had allowed me to move back into my old room, where I routinely collapsed after getting home from the office well after midnight. Professional life was punishing, but I gave it my all. For a brief time, I felt like I was flying: at my first performance review, I was told I had ‘partner potential’.

But then I got a phone call, telling me that one of the senior American partners wanted to meet me. That was unusual; but then again, I’d been working so hard and getting such good feedback, I figured it couldn’t be anything too bad. I was directed to an office on the first floor, several levels below where I usually sat.

After he fired me, my ears buzzed and my chest tightened; I don’t remember much else, except being told that I shouldn’t even return to my desk. It became apparent that the location of the meeting had been chosen because it would allow me to take a single flight of stairs down to the ground floor. No one would need to see me, and I wouldn’t need to speak to anyone.

The decision felt cruel and unfair. But more than anything, it seemed to violate the laws that for many years had been my way of making sense of the world: the laws of physics. Cause and effect, action and reaction. What followed was an unlikely journey – one in which the equations I thought I’d left behind at university became, unexpectedly, a companion through the messiest parts of life.

Before work, before university, I attended a competitive and prestigious all-boys school in London. While I’ll be forever grateful for the opportunities my education afforded me, life still felt tough for me as a lonely and anxious teenager. The school’s social currency was confidence, quick comebacks, and an effortless cool I never quite mastered. I often felt like I was watching from the edges, trying to decode the rules of a game that everyone else grasped intuitively.

The only thing that got me through was physics. The most fundamental of the sciences, physics represented a world that was perfectly ordered. It offered structure, rules and predictability. There was no social speculation; I could just work hard and try to figure things out. Problems and solutions, equations and outcomes. It didn’t matter how popular I was – what mattered was whether I understood the system. Slowly, the chaos of the world developed a sense of form and structure.

That clarity stayed with me, through school and into university. I read physics at Oxford, convinced for a long time that I wanted to become a scientist. It wasn’t always easy; there were late nights, bitter struggles with problem sets, moments I wondered if I’d ever get it. But when it clicked, it was wonderful: entropy, quantum mechanics, cosmology, all those deep, strange laws that govern the Universe. Physics seemed like it had a purpose, and I thought we’d go the distance.

But at some point in my final year at university, things started to change. Physics still fascinated me, but I found myself drawn to other subjects too – politics, economics, business. I wanted to understand not just how the Universe worked, but how people did. So after graduating, I decided to leave physics behind and see where those other interests would take me.

For the first time in years, physics seems to be at the heart of the cultural zeitgeist

As it turns out, when I stepped away from physics, many others did too. In the years after I left university at the turn of the millennium, physics began to fade from view in the English classroom. In 2006, physics A-level entries (post-16 qualifications in the UK) were down 37 per cent from where they were in 1991. The absolute numbers have since rebounded – but not for everyone. Today, the gender gap remains stark: only 23 per cent of A-level physics entries in 2026 came from girls, a figure that hasn’t budged much in decades. And more than half of GCSE physics classes in England (taken by 14- to 16-year-olds) are taught by a non-specialist, with a shortage of some 3,500 physics teachers nationally.

Research looking at why students choose or reject physics has found that it’s seen as abstract, difficult, and disconnected from real life – a perception that’s remained steady, even as enrolment has recovered. Meanwhile, newer fields – computer science, behavioural economics, even data journalism – have felt more immediate, more applicable. They speak the language of now.

What’s strange is that this perception problem has happened at the same historical moment in which physics has begun popping up in other surprising places.

Dominic Cummings, the strategist behind Brexit and later Boris Johnson’s chief adviser, gave physics a fair share of the credit for the success of his campaigns. In one of his highly popular newsletters, he paraphrased the theoretical physicist Richard Feynman: ‘The most important thing is not to fool yourself and you are the easiest person to fool.’ Then there’s Elon Musk, who credits the success of his many business ventures to physics and ‘first-principles thinking’: discard convention, start from fundamental truths. And for decades, the legendary investor Charlie Munger made the same case in finance, saying that the ‘logic and power’ of physics had helped him enormously.

For the first time in years, physics seems to be at the heart of the cultural zeitgeist, praised by public figures whose decisions affect millions of lives. But look closer, and the picture is more complicated.

In the first instance, billionaires and political operatives make for awkward ambassadors; Cummings, Musk and Munger might be brilliant, but they’re also extremely divisive. But more than who they are, what interests me is how they’re putting physics to work – whether they’re truly thinking with the discipline, or just brandishing it for rhetorical effect. Is ‘physics’ simply a shorthand for cutting through complexity, for stripping down problems to their most basic parts? Or does it genuinely offer something distinctive that other sciences and ways of thinking cannot?

Philosophers call the first approach ‘reductionism’: the idea that if you break any system into small enough components and trace them far enough, you eventually arrive at physics. That view can be powerful, and explains why so many people find it attractive.

It’s also been spectacularly successful. When 19th-century physicists showed that heat was simply the motion of atoms – that temperature, seemingly its own phenomenon, was actually just particles bouncing faster – an entire science collapsed into physics. Years later, that same approach helped particle physicists break matter into smaller and smaller pieces until arriving at something apparently irreducible. From the reductionist instinct came quarks, leptons and the Higgs boson. Their catalogue blueprint, the Standard Model, remains one of the greatest intellectual achievements in human history.

But reductionism has its limits. Take politics: a radical reductionist might say that this too comes down to physics, because politics is about the behaviour of groups of people; groups are made of individual people; people are made of atoms; atoms are governed by physics. But does this mean that we could predict the outcome of, say, a national election by studying the behaviour of individual atoms inside the brains of every registered voter? Unlikely. Putting aside issues of practicality, what would be the point? Economists already have economics. Psychologists already have psychology. Politicians have political theory. Physics has value only if it’s additive and illuminating.

For me, the real value of physics had never been as a cudgel for smashing things up into their smallest bits, but as a framework for navigating systems – for recognising patterns, probing assumptions, and testing whether the models we rely on actually work as they’re meant to. We see this way of thinking throughout the history of science. When cholera swept through Soho in 1854, the physician John Snow didn’t know its cause. But he mapped the cases, identified the pattern, and traced the outbreak to a single water pump on Broad Street. The founder of what we now know as epidemiology, Snow worked by constructing and interrogating mental models of the world, probing their assumptions, and following the data wherever they led.

The question, then, is not simply whether physics can be borrowed as rhetoric, but whether it really helps us to see the world more clearly, in ways that complement and benefit other disciplines. That, at least, was what stayed with me after I stopped studying it formally. Not equations or textbooks, but a way of thinking that I found myself reaching for when my world was falling apart.

Getting fired was one of those moments. I had worked so hard, yet somehow I’d still failed. Everything I understood about cause and effect told me this shouldn’t have happened. But here I was, after months of working flat out, with nothing to show for it.

An infinitesimally small shift in starting positions for the three objects can throw the whole system off balance

While some might have turned to therapy or career counselling, I turned back to physics to try to move on. The immediate cause was clear enough. The dot-com bubble had burst, sending ripples across the global economy that eventually reached my desk. Belts tightened, and the harsh rule in such circumstances tends to be last in, first out.

The dot-com bust was not the first nor last time something like this would happen. In 2008 came the subprime mortgage crisis; in 2011, the eurozone crashed; in 2013, the rupee tanked; in 2015, there was turbulence on the Chinese stock market; and in 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic. All these crises had two things in common. First, almost no one saw them coming – at least not precisely when or where or how. Second, they weren’t triggered by some enormous dramatic collapse, but by small, seemingly innocuous failures that cascaded into something far larger. For example, it just took a few small incidents that might otherwise have passed unnoticed – like the failure of a local mortgage lender in Southern California – to precipitate the subprime mortgage crisis.

All these events are examples of what physicists might call chaotic systems – deterministic in theory, but in practice so sensitive to initial conditions that tiny variations can spiral into radically different outcomes. A well-known example is the ‘three-body problem’, popularised by Liu Cixin’s 2008 novel of the same name and a 2024 Netflix adaptation. If you have two planets orbiting each other, you can write down neat equations to predict their paths forever. But add a third planet, and suddenly the maths explodes into unpredictability. The three bodies are still governed by clear laws, but an infinitesimally small shift in starting positions for the three objects can throw the whole system off balance.

The mathematician Edward Lorenz discovered something similar in 1961 when running weather simulations. His first attempt entered starting values rounded to six decimal places. His second try was rounded only to three. Yet the results diverged so dramatically that he initially suspected it was a computer fault. In fact, tiny differences in initial conditions had cascaded into entirely different weather systems. The atmosphere, like the economy, like a career, was deterministic in principle and unpredictable in practice.

As a young graduate, I had been living without surge capacity. In truth, most of us do

Understanding the crash was one thing, but physics also helped me think about what came next. I had believed that inputs led to proportional outcomes; logically, in that world, the way to get ahead was to work as hard as possible. But physics teaches that chaotic systems play by different rules. They call instead for surge capacity, an extra buffer that allows them to absorb shocks. Without it, even small failures can lead to total collapse.

Think of a power grid. Most of the time it hums along without problem. But during an unexpected surge, such as a heatwave when millions of air conditioners are switched on at once, the system can overload and shut down. To prevent this, engineers design grids with slack in the system and extra capacity to handle unexpected spikes. Without it, a minor disruption can cascade into a blackout.

That was my mistake. As a young graduate, I had been living without surge capacity. In truth, most of us do. We optimise everything from our schedules to our to-do lists – convinced that if we just push a bit harder, we’ll be fine. But the more we operate at our limits, the more fragile we become.

Physics provides a different lesson. Rather than relentlessly maximising, resilience is about building the capacity to withstand outlier events when they come. That might mean time slack, leaving space in our lives to recover rather than scheduling every minute. It might mean career slack, developing new skills, side projects and networks, rather than relying on a single path. Surge capacity might not prevent a crisis, but it sure helps survive one.

After my brief and bruising spell in consulting, I joined the civil service and spent most of the rest of my 20s working in government. I loved the sense of purpose, the colleagues and the privilege of shaping policy. Yet, if I’m honest, I still carried a small canker of resentment and jealousy towards my former consulting colleagues.

Compared with the UK national average, I know I was paid well as a civil servant. But with friends on six-figure salaries, it felt like I was failing at something. They could afford nicer clothes, cars and apartments. And then there was the magic trick of turning money into more money by buying assets, further widening the gap between their bank balances and mine. What stung wasn’t the inequality itself, but the perceived unfairness of the circumstances. I felt like I’d worked just as hard and still fallen behind. That distinction between inequality and unfairness became important to me.

Psychologists have shown that we’re wired to make this distinction from a very young age. In one Yale study, children were asked to split 10 coins between two people based on their performance on a task. When the two people performed equally, the children split the coins five-five – equal and fair. When one person did better, the children split the coins six-four – unequal but still fair. The interesting result happened when the children were told that both people had performed equally, but they now had to split 11 coins. With no way to maintain fairness, what could the children do? They decided to simply throw away one coin. Time and again, the children prioritised fairness.

People will accept a world where some have more, so long as they believe the game isn’t rigged

This distinction is also evident in physics. Inequality, in the literal sense of unevenness, is built into the fabric of the Universe. In the very beginning, the cosmos was smooth and equal, a uniform fog. Only when tiny imperfections appeared – quantum fluctuations that allowed matter to clump in some places more than others – did galaxies, stars and planets emerge. Without that inequality, there would have been no structure, no possibility of life. In that sense, inequality is not always a flaw. Sometimes it is the condition for growth and diversity.

We see the same principle in natural systems. Rivers branch into unequal tributaries. Lungs and blood vessels evolve into networks with a few large arteries feeding many smaller ones. That inequality of size isn’t corruption or greed, but a kind of efficiency. It allows flow. Yet when the flow is blocked, like when a river silts up or a vessel clogs, the system fails. The problem, in other words, is not inequality itself, but unfairness: the obstruction of flow, the stacking of rules, the blocking of opportunity.

I think this is true in human systems, too. A society where some are richer than others may be tolerable, even healthy, so long as opportunities and resources can still move freely. But a society where opportunity is blocked, where the rules are stacked, where unfairness rules – people reject that instinctively. Just as I did when I looked at my friends’ consulting careers and wondered why I’d been cast out. Physics, then, suggests that a lack of justice is the real problem, rather than inequality per se. People will accept a world where some have more, so long as they believe the game isn’t rigged.

Suddenly I saw this dynamic about fairness everywhere I looked. The financial crisis of 2007-08 wasn’t just about banks making risky bets, but about the perception that ordinary people paid the price while bankers walked away with bonuses intact. The eurozone crisis wasn’t just about debt, but about southern European countries being squeezed by rules they hadn’t set. The Occupy protests, the Arab Spring, Brexit, Donald Trump – all, in their different ways, were rebellions against unfairness.

Looking at the world through a physicist’s lens, these moments resemble phase transitions. You can heat water gradually and nothing seems to change – until you reach a critical threshold, a boiling point, and suddenly the whole system transforms from liquid to gas. Human societies, too, can bear strain for a while. But once unfairness feels systemic, the pressure builds until the system flips.

Small wonder, then, that in an age of tumult and transition, physics has found new admirers – especially among those who want to catalyse radical change, for better or worse. Musk speaks of first principles, Cummings of complexity. Their examples show how the tools of physics can shape thinking far beyond the laboratory. But in their hands, physics can feel more like a weapon than a framework, a way of bulldozing nuance in the name of clarity. For the rest of us, the challenge is not simply to borrow the garb and glamour of physics, but to carry forward its mindset – one that values humility as much as boldness, and curiosity as much as certainty.

That, I think, is where physics can still make its greatest contribution. Not by giving us ready-made answers or comforting illusions of inevitability, but by training us to question ourselves and live with the resulting uncertainty. Public discourse is saturated with physics, yet we need a deeper grounding in what it really teaches us about how to ask better questions, to test our own blind spots, and to admit what we don’t know. That need feels more urgent as new technologies only increase the temptation to reach for shortcuts.

We need artists who understand systems, scientists who can tell stories, leaders who can hold both

So what would it take to embed this shift? My journey with physics began when I was a teenager, and that’s where I believe we need to start now. Too often, we present physics to young people as dry and technical. We teach them equations but not frameworks, facts without wonder. We rarely tell them that physics can help with the messiest parts of life, bound up as they are with uncertainty, resilience, decision-making.

In the UK, we make things worse by forcing students to choose just three or four subjects to study for the final two years of school. In practice, this often forces a split between being on the ‘science’ track or the ‘arts’ track. That false binary deprives us of exactly the kind of multidisciplinary thinkers we need: artists who understand systems, scientists who can tell stories, leaders who can hold both.

When I visit schools now, I try to show physics as a kind of superpower. I want young people to feel that physics is something they can use, not something that excludes them. More than anything, I want them to feel it’s theirs.

I started this essay as a young man being shown the door by a superior. I ended it somewhere else entirely, with physics as a way of making sense of the messiest parts of life. But, really, what I’ve been edging up to is a story about how certain hardwon habits of mind can help us find meaning in the messiness and unpredictability of reality. For those of us who are not professional scientists, maybe the real task isn’t to love physics uncritically, or wield it carelessly, but to use it wisely. Physics shouldn’t be a shortcut to rock-solid certainty, so much as a way to live more humanely without it.

item.title: The Amarna letters
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
Petty disputes, pleas for help and requests for gold – explore letters sent to Egyptian pharaohs more than 3,000 years ago

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded: First discovered in Egypt in the late 19th century, the collection of clay tablets known as the Amarna letters is one of our richest windows into the ancient world. The letters are extraordinary not only for their contents – diplomatic communications exchanged between Egyptian pharaohs and other nearby rulers in the 14th century BCE – but also for their script: they were written not in Egyptian hieroglyphs but largely in cuneiform, a writing system most often associated with ancient Mesopotamia. In this video from the British Museum, the always entertaining Assyriologist Irving Finkel details how the letters came to be and how they were discovered, and delves into the fascinating correspondence itself, which includes petty disputes over perceived slights, leaders lobbying for military support and more than a few requests for gold.

item.title: Love with nowhere to go
item.dc:creator: Derek van Zoonen
item.description:
Grief is not only for the dead. When we are unable to honour other profound losses, we become strangers to ourselves

- by Derek van Zoonen

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

23 minute listen

I have been grieving my mother for years, even though she is still alive. Sometimes before falling asleep – in that liminal space between waking and sleeping where the self becomes porous – I’d see the image of the sweet and caring woman who would come to say goodnight, her cheeks covered in thick layers of night cream. Then, out of nowhere, the image would flip into the raging woman who was so entangled in her own suffering that she turned her frustration on us. Over the years, that second woman slowly swallowed the first, as she got pulled into my brother’s addiction. It’s hard to say where her own unhappiness ended and my brother’s suffering began, but together they drifted into a parallel reality, cut off from the world beyond their heads. There was no funeral for this. No condolence cards. No flowers. No phone calls. No leave of absence. What was I supposed to mourn?

And yet what I felt for them, what I still feel, has the unmistakable gravity of mourning. Can there be grief without death? I have come to think that we grieve much more often than we realise, and that death is grief’s most visible occasion rather than its essence. If that doesn’t match your experience, it may be because we rarely call these other losses by their name. Most of our losses arrive without a funeral. That is the human predicament: we are creatures built to attach, living in a world where nothing stays. Sooner or later, we lose the things we care about. And since we are complex beings with a body, a mind, a community and an environment – beings who love many different things – there is a great deal we can lose, from our physical health to our sense of who we are, from relationships to homelands to the natural world we share with other species. For creatures like us, there is no way around heartbreak: to live is to lose. Grief is what love does when its object is gone. It is love with nowhere to go.

Over the past few years I have accumulated many such losses. There is the psychological loss of my father as I knew and loved him: a brutal stroke rendered him incapable of walking and cycling, and cycling was the only thing that could ‘make his thoughts liquid’, as he used to say. There is the loss of old friendships. First you are no longer part of each other’s lives – you just update one another about your life – and then, one day, it becomes awkward to reach out at all. There is the gradual softening of an academic identity I’d spent the most vital years of my life constructing. It was a genuine vocation, a life of the mind that taught me to think slowly and carefully. But it was also, as I came to realise, a way of living safely at one remove from where actual life takes place. What is slipping away is a future in which being an academic philosopher would be the whole answer to the question of who I am.

There was the woman whose calmness, clarity and silence embodied the qualities I have come to like so much about the Nordics since moving to Norway. Like a magical stranger, she entered my life unexpectedly, but at the same time her arrival felt so natural, her presence so obvious, that it was as if she had always been there. After our first meeting, which lasted almost 24 hours, I wrote in my journal: Ze is gekomen om te blijven. ‘She had come to stay.’ And she did, for nine intense months. She tried to teach me to ski. We listened to the music of Nils Frahm, which reminded her of melting snow. And she made me see that the deepest form of intimacy happens in the space between the words.

But despite the depth of our bond, she left, abruptly, as if she had never been there. She had fallen in love with another man. I was left behind, dazed and disoriented, and although my heart was broken, this kind of loss did not have a name that matched how shattered I felt. It was ‘just a breakup’, and it didn’t even deserve that name: we had been dating, but it never technically became a relationship. It was also a romantic connection that ran alongside another one, a long partnership that was open by mutual agreement and conscious design. Much about it wasn’t legible to most people around me. I faced the grief largely by myself. No scripts, no rituals, no recognised form, no legitimacy, no shared language, no way to make sense of what had happened to me.

Part of what made the experience so disorienting was a narrow idea of what grief is. In psychology, in philosophy and in our Western culture at large, grief has been treated almost exclusively as a response to the death of someone we love. It’s a neat, tidy understanding. The most celebrated grief memoirs – think of The Year of Magical Thinking (2005) by Joan Didion and A Grief Observed (1961) by C S Lewis – are concerned with the loss of a life partner. And Michael Cholbi’s Grief: A Philosophical Guide (2021) – one of the most extensive philosophical treatments of the emotion – focuses mostly on the grief we experience at the death of someone we love or who otherwise matters to us.

Restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches

Death is visible and final: it has a body, a date, a medical certificate. The other losses are blurrier: they have no physical object, no clear beginning or end, no tangible proof they happened. We also have an infrastructure for death: funerals, condolence cards, flowers, casseroles, bereavement leave – a whole social script. Perhaps the infrastructure defines what counts: if there is no social and cultural scaffolding to digest the experience, it must not be real grief.

The prime reason for the single-minded focus on death loss, however, must be that bereavement is simply the most striking instance of a broader emotional phenomenon that comes in degrees. But restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches, anxiety to panic attacks, sadness to depression, or pleasure to ecstasy – it is taking the most extreme instantiation of something and making it the essence of that thing.

If grief isn’t just about death, what is it about? What do all these cases of grief share? A good way to answer this question starts from the observation that every emotion has a characteristic thing it is about. Fear is about danger or threat; anger is about offence or injustice; happiness and joy are about flourishing or harmony between self and world. What is grief about? If you say ‘death’, you are doing something weird: you are defining the emotion by the particular thing that sets it off, rather than by what that thing means to us. In technical philosophical jargon, you are making the mistake of conflating an emotion’s material object with its formal object. Fear of sharks, fear of public speaking and fear of heights aren’t three different emotions – shark-fear, public-speaking-fear and heights-fear. All three count as fear because they are about danger: their aim is to tell you something is threatening.

Grief clearly has something to do with loss. Although this gets us somewhere, it doesn’t get us far enough. Mere loss is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a pen or an old sweater, I am not experiencing any grief. If I have any emotional reaction at all, it will be a slight ripple of annoyance. Perhaps we should add that for there to be grief we must lose something we care about or love, but, again, this is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a book I really like or don’t get a dream job I applied for, what I experience is frustration or disappointment, sadness perhaps, but not grief.

What sets grief apart is how deeply the loss reaches into the fabric of your life: grief begins where your identity is disrupted. What is lost in the case of grief is not just some concrete, historical object, but a cluster of (future) possibilities that are tightly woven into your sense of identity, life structure or experiential world. When they go, you don’t just lose something: you lose a version of yourself, your life is turned upside down, and you come to inhabit, in a real sense, a different world. This is why death is grief’s most extreme instance, rather than its only one. When someone we love dies, every possibility – not only our own possibilities with them, but their possibilities too – is wiped out. As Matthew Ratcliffe and Louise Richardson, academic philosophers at the University of York, put it in their paper ‘Grief Over Non-Death Losses: A Phenomenological Perspective’ (2023):

Grief is thus distinctive insofar as it involves recognising and comprehending the implications of lost possibilities for the structure of one’s life or world, and – over time – coming to reorganise one’s life accordingly.

This reorganisation is not merely cognitive. It lives in many other places: in the body (the hand that still reaches for the phone to text someone who no longer answers your messages), in how you experience your surroundings (the café you used to visit together that now feels alien or even hostile), or in your autobiographical memories (the shared joke that simply doesn’t land with other people).

‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to’

My mother is still alive. No one has died: there is no concrete, historical object that has been pulled beyond my grasp. But a whole set of possibilities that had been woven into the structure of my life and world, all bound up with having a mother who was present, responsive, good enough – those are gone. It has become impossible to call her and poke that mind of hers, so unusually free and unusually deep.

The same goes for my father. Sure, he survived the stroke. But the man whose restless mind needed to cycle to make his thoughts liquid – the future I had with that man, the shared cycling trips in the south of France, the conversations that needed repetitive, cyclical movement to come alive – that future was negated. The same structure holds for the woman whose disappearance collapsed an experiential world that felt like a home I had only just found, and for the academic identity I had built over almost two decades. As other vocations began to call more insistently, a single, all-consuming way of being in the world – the thinker, the life of the mind, the person whose future would be organised around reading and writing – loosened its hold.

The case that makes this way of thinking about grief most compelling, though, is one where there is no concrete object of loss at all. Ratcliffe and Richardson’s central example is involuntary childlessness – grief for a child who never was, a future that was imagined, anticipated and deeply woven into one’s sense of self, but that never materialised. Here, no one died and no one left. There is nothing tangible to point to: no grave, no anniversary, no recorded name, no memorial service, no shared practices to give words or meaning to the loss. And yet, as one respondent in their study put it: ‘No one can understand what it’s like to carry this loss. In their minds, no baby meant no loss.’ Another respondent simply called their grief by its name: ‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to.’ And a third spoke, chillingly, of ‘the death of a future life’.

They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience

‘No baby meant no loss.’ Many forms of non-death loss are what the family therapist Pauline Boss calls ‘ambiguous loss’. These are losses without clear boundaries, without a definite beginning or end – cases where someone is physically present but psychologically gone, or physically gone but psychologically still there. Think of an Alzheimer’s patient whose self has been erased by the disease or of a soldier missing in action. Because many non-death losses are ambiguous, the grief that follows them is not openly acknowledged, socially validated or publicly mourned – what the grief scholar Kenneth Doka has called ‘disenfranchised grief’.

Those whose grief is disenfranchised because their losses are ambiguous don’t just lack scripts or rituals or traditions. They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience. When we lack the concepts to name what it is like to be us, what it is we are going through, we suffer what the philosopher Miranda Fricker calls a ‘hermeneutical injustice’ – an inability to make our own experience intelligible to ourselves and to others. This is not because we are confused, but because the shared language or conceptual apparatus – the frameworks we use to make sense of ourselves – hasn’t caught up. As two of Ratcliffe and Richardson’s respondents put it: ‘It took me a while to understand that what I was feeling was grief’; ‘I never realised this was grief until I found others in a similar situation.’

The same happened to me: when the magical stranger disappeared, my loss was ambiguous – she still existed, we were never officially together, I had another partner – and my grief went into hiding. In a culture where the end of a relationship is ‘just a breakup’ and monogamy is the unspoken rule, I lacked the rituals to digest the grief and the hermeneutical resources to conceptualise and communicate what had happened to me. For ‘self-interpreting animals’ like us, in the words of the philosopher Charles Taylor, the result is that we end up in the dark, as strangers to ourselves.

The narrowing of grief to bereavement is more than a conceptual mistake. It does real damage. What the writer and grief counsellor Stephen Levine called ‘unattended sorrow’ doesn’t dissolve but goes underground, hiding in the shadows, later resurfacing as unexpected symptoms. I have been there. A mechanical tightness in the chest and a hard belly, like wearing a harness to brace against life. Harrowing dreams. Attempts to numb what is too painful to feel alone. And, worst of all, cynicism and a slow erosion of trust. Not just in other people, but in your own feelings, your own intuitions about the depth, sustainability and future of any new connection. When no one around you recognises your grief, you begin to wonder whether you were wrong to feel it at all.

Sigmund Freud understood this, though he read it as pathology. In the essay ‘Mourning and Melancholia’ (1917), he contended that grief is healthy and normal, but only if it is intelligible and bounded. The job of mourning, he argued, is to detach you from the lost object and reinvest your emotional energy elsewhere. If you can’t complete that job, if the loss is unclear or unnamed or ambiguous, you are no longer mourning. Instead, you are suffering from an illness called melancholia. For Freud, grief that cannot do its work calcifies into something darker, something more elusive.

If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to themselves

But the damage runs deeper than that. When we cannot grieve a loss, we lose something else along with it: the chance to register what mattered to us. Grief is how we come to know what we loved in the presence of its absence. Or as the psychotherapist and grief worker Francis Weller puts it in The Wild Edge of Sorrow (2015):

Grief and love are sisters, woven together from the beginning. Their kinship reminds us that there is no love that does not contain loss and no loss that is not a reminder of the love we carry for what we once held close.

Your grief tells you that you had the courage to love, that you allowed someone or something else to enter ‘the core of [your] being and find a home in [your] heart’. If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to what they loved and valued, which is to say that you deny them access to themselves. You don’t just rob them, then, of their love; you also rob them of self-knowledge.

The tradition I spent most of my life in – the lineage of Western thinkers who asked how a human being should live – was the first place I looked to understand what was happening to me. These thinkers had a lot to say about grief, but most of it was suspicious and sceptical. Plato believed a good man is the most self-sufficient of all, and least shaken by loss. In the Phaedo, Socrates’ wife Xanthippe is led away wailing before the philosophy can begin, and towards the end of the dialogue, Socrates rebukes his weeping friends for behaving like women. A similar sentiment can be found among the Stoics. Epictetus, in the Enchiridion, compares the loss of a wife or child to a jug breaking. And Marcus Aurelius, who lost many of his own children, reminds himself in his Meditations not to pray that he might keep his child, but to pray that he might not fear losing him.

Behind this way of thinking lies an expensive belief: that attachment is a liability, and that a wise person – someone who has figured out how to live the best possible life – does not need anything that can be taken away from him. If grief is love with nowhere to go, a tradition that treated such love as an error was never going to know what to do with it.

Christianity kept the verdict the ancients had arrived at. In his Confessions (397-400 CE), Saint Augustine looks back on his devastation after a friend’s death, and diagnoses it as a spiritual mistake: ‘Why had that grief penetrated me so easily and so deeply, if not because I had poured out my soul onto the sand, loving someone who would die as if he never would?’ Baruch Spinoza – not religious in any conventional sense of the word – reached the same conclusion. Sadness, he writes in his Ethics (1677), is the mind’s move to a lesser perfection, a loss of its power to act. This means it can never be a good in itself, and its typical source is too much love for things that are impermanent. The cure for grief – and this puts him squarely back into the ancient intellectualist tradition – is understanding: the moment it dawns on us that what we lost could never have been kept, our grief will relax.

The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder

Arthur Schopenhauer, unlike many before him, did not despise grief. In The World as Will and Representation (1818), he values sorrow for one reason only: great personal suffering breaks the will and leads to self-renunciation (Selbstverneinung). Grief is worth having, then, because it has the power to cure us of wanting the world at all, which means that, in the end, he is not so far from the thinkers who came before him. A good life, for all of them, is a matter of loosening our attachments to what is impermanent and fragile.

What began as a doctrine of philosophers leaked into the wider culture. In his landmark study Death, Grief, and Mourning in Contemporary Britain (1965), the anthropologist Geoffrey Gorer found that mourning was increasingly seen as ‘a weakness, a self-indulgence, a reprehensible bad habit instead of as a psychological necessity’. In the 1970s, the historian Philippe Ariès traced the same shift across the industrial West: death, once familiar, had become shameful, something to be hidden. Meanwhile, medicine had entered the debate. In 1961, the psychiatrist George Engel asked, half provocatively, whether grief was a disease. In 2000, the philosopher Stephen Wilkinson answered: yes. In one of academic philosophy’s leading journals, he argued that even normal, healthy grief qualifies as a mental disorder because it meets the standard definition of one. Like all mental disorders, it involves significant distress and interrupts normal functioning. In 2013, the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders removed the clause that had excluded the recently bereaved from receiving a diagnosis of major depressive disorder. Then, in 2022, the revised edition added prolonged grief disorder, whose possible symptoms include identity disruption, such as the feeling that part of oneself has died. The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder – though, tellingly, only when someone has actually died.

But the Western tradition had it backwards. Suppressing, eradicating, denying or pathologising grief doesn’t protect the good life; it sabotages human flourishing by cutting us off from the things we love. More than that, it cuts us off from each other. Grief named and disclosed is grief that can be met, grief that can be placed between you and another person, where the two of you can look at it and hold it together. That shared vulnerability lets one person recognise another in their common humanity. Grief, as Weller reminds us, was never meant to be carried alone; it was meant to be held and processed by a whole village. Strip it of its name and you strip people of the possibility of being seen in their loss, of discovering that the wound they thought was theirs alone is in fact shared by those around them.

Recently, while in the Netherlands, I visited the Kröller-Müller Museum with my father, the same father whose future was negated by a stroke. I looked at him from a distance, the man who once built his life around cycling – to France, to Rome, to Spain’s Santiago de Compostela – now hunched behind his rollator. We stood together in front of Vincent van Gogh’s painting At Eternity’s Gate (1890): an old man, face buried in his fists, clearly hurting. A sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man painted by a sorrowful man. Years before he painted it, when he first drew the same figure for a lithograph, Van Gogh wrote that there can be an ‘unutterably moving’ quality, ‘something precious, something noble’, in the expression of an old man like that.

I didn’t know my father loved Van Gogh as much as I do. We stood there for a long time – somehow in contact with the magic of grief – and something opened up between us that had no name but felt important, exquisitely alive. We didn’t talk about my mother, or how our family had unravelled, or what the stroke had taken from him. We didn’t have to. The painting said what neither of us could.

item.title: Great art explained: Tamara in the green Bugatti
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
A very modern conception of womanhood: in the Jazz Age paintings of Tamara de Lempicka, women were bold, free and stylish

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded: The Polish painter Tamara de Lempicka (1894-1980) was a defining figure of Art Deco: an aesthetic movement of the early 20th century that fused modernist geometry with excitement and glamour to capture a new faith in progress. Her paintings frequently convey unapologetic female autonomy and desire amid the Jazz Age. In this instalment of the YouTube series Great Art Explained, the curator and video essayist James Payne and the art historian Laura Beardsell-Moore explore how Lempicka’s life and times shaped her work – from her affluent upbringing and flight from the Russian Revolution to her experience in 1920s Paris. In particular, they dissect how her most famous painting, Autoportrait (Tamara in the Green Bugatti) (1929), depicted nothing less than a new, deeply modern conception of womanhood.

item.title: How to build real peace
item.dc:creator: Azize Aslan
item.description:
From Colombia to Syria, I’ve seen that capitalist logic can’t help to rebuild postwar countries but cooperatives can

- by Azize Aslan

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

27 minute listen

When I was seven years old, my family was forced to flee escalating violence. We left Bakur – a Kurdish region in what is currently southeastern Turkey – for a city further west, where we worked in Turkish fields, living in a tent until we could save up to rent a house on the city margins, in a neighbourhood with no electricity or road access. Those are some of my earliest memories of everyday violence against people like me.

For centuries, my ancestors had lived in relative harmony with other communities. But, with the emergence of modern nation-states in the region, Kurdistan – the traditional homeland of the Kurds – was fractured into southeastern Turkey, northern Iraq, northwestern Iran, and northeastern Syria. A violent assimilation was imposed upon us. For more than a century, Kurdish people have been denied recognition as a nation, their language banned, erased from maps, stripped of citizenship rights, and dispossessed of their lands. For my generation, therefore, freedom was never an abstract political matter; armed struggle was often seen as a necessity to achieve it. Even so, national liberation movements always sought dialogue with the states they fought against. I grew up inside that insistence, carrying the hope of a dignified peace.

In 2013, after almost three decades of war, peace talks were held between the Turkish state and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), which first sought an independent Kurdish state and, later, autonomy and increased political and cultural rights for Kurds within Turkey. In 2015, these collapsed. War returned to Kurdistan and, with it, the persecution of everyone who had staked something on that possibility of peace. This included me. I was a doctoral student at the time, researching economic autonomy in Kurdistan, and it became clear that this work would no longer be tenable in the new political climate. I moved to Latin America, to complete my doctoral studies and study revolutionary movements in that part of the world, grappling all the while with a question that had become inseparable from my own existence: how could peace be built in Kurdistan?

The academic literature on peace told me I might find an answer in Guatemala. Between 1960 and 1996, civil war had ravaged the country, killing more than 200,000 people and displacing more than a million – more than a 10th of the total population. The conflict – which began as an uprising against extreme inequality, particularly in land ownership, and systemic discrimination against the Maya people – had turned the state into a counterinsurgency apparatus, powered by paramilitary death squads and a doctrine of the ‘internal enemy’ that erased the line between combatant and civilian. Against this backdrop, the Acuerdo de Paz Firme y Duradera (Agreement on a Firm and Lasting Peace) was both celebrated and touted as innovative when it was signed in 1996. The agreement broke ground by confronting the past directly: the Commission for Historical Clarification investigated the atrocities committed during the civil war, most of them attributable to the state, and, unusually, partly as a result of its findings, heads of state were later tried for war crimes.

But it was soon apparent that the peace accord had failed to address the problems that led to the conflict in the first place. The guerilla fighters who returned to their villages – or who had to reinvent themselves in cities where no one was waiting for them – found intact the system they had been unable to transform through armed struggle: poverty. Today, Guatemala remains one of the most unequal countries in Latin America vis-à-vis class, ethnicity and gender. The deepest wound of the war – land tenure – was never resolved: no equitable land redistribution took place after the 1996 accords. In fact, as the World Bank researchers Caroline Moser and Cathy McIlwaine have noted: ‘Guatemala has become a substantially more violent country since the end of the internal armed conflict.’

One ex-combatant had joined the insurgency as a 13-year-old and stayed in the mountains until the peace accord was signed. I met him in 2017, more than 20 years after the formal end to the war, at the community radio project he had built near Xela, in the western highlands of Guatemala. ‘Despite the deaths and the hardship of the war, I never cried,’ he told me. ‘But the day the war ended, I cried – because I didn’t know how to live in peace: I had no home, no job, no trade. And I asked myself: what now?’

Peace, as currently practised, doesn’t break the cycle of injustice that leads to war in the first place

I had come to Guatemala searching for an answer to my own political and existential preoccupations but it was the ex-combatant’s question – What now? – that stayed with me, an accusation directed at the very concept of peace he had been promised.

Guatemala is not an anomaly in this regard. Since the end of the Cold War, more than 30 comprehensive peace agreements have been signed around the world but few, if any, have succeeded in building a durable peace. Accords signed under the dominant peacebuilding paradigm focus almost exclusively on stopping direct violence through ceasefires, weapons handovers, disarmament, individual reintegration, all on the assumption that democratic institutions and free markets will naturally produce lasting peace. But peace, as currently practised, doesn’t break the cycle of injustice that leads to war in the first place.

The sociologist Johan Galtung, often described as the founder of peace and conflict studies, distinguished between ‘negative peace’ – the absence of direct violence – and ‘positive peace’, which requires dismantling the structures of injustice that fuel conflict. The typical approach to peace in post-conflict contexts is encapsulated in the United Nations’ classic disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration model, first implemented by its peacekeeping operations in El Salvador in 1989 and used in more than 30 countries since. Under this strategy, former combatants are required to surrender their weapons and disband their command structures, and are entitled to short-term stipends and training that will facilitate their reintegration into civilian economic life. This approach was also implemented in Guatemala.

But what neither Galtung nor other sophisticated theorists of a liberal framework for peace tend to question is whether capitalist relations of production can lead to peace when this is itself a structural source of violence. They propose reforms, redistribution, greater inclusion – but all within the same system that armed struggles in places like Guatemala sought to transform. As a sociologist interested in revolutionary social movements, what I have observed in my fieldwork in Guatemala, Colombia and northern Syria has led me to a more radical conclusion: real peace requires building economies that operate on an entirely different logic from that of capital – not just in postwar communities but more widely, because we all need more peace in our daily lives.

Cooperatives are one mechanism through which a different economic logic, one more conducive to a durable peace, can take root. In the language of the International Cooperative Alliance – an association established in 1895 when the concept, while as old as time itself, seemed to be gaining traction in Europe – cooperatives are collective entities established by people who come together to address common economic and social needs. They are founded on principles of democracy and autonomy, and built on voluntary participation and solidarity. From the Rochdale weavers of northern England in 1844 – often regarded as the forebears of modern cooperatives – to present-day credit unions, the cooperative movement has produced both genuinely emancipatory experiments and organisations that simply reproduce market logic under a different name. Cooperativism is also central to democratic confederalism, a political theory put forth by Abdullah Öcalan, one of the PKK’s founding members. It was through reading Öcalan that I became interested in the emancipatory potential of cooperatives.

A form of self-determination oriented towards the autonomy of all peoples, particularly women, democratic confederalism proposes a structure of governance organised from the bottom up. In Öcalan’s paradigm, cooperatives are the means through which an economy in service of these principles – communal, ecological, feminist – might be built. The cooperatives that interest me, therefore, have three defining characteristics: they are part of broader social movements and territorial struggles; they prioritise meeting collective needs over the accumulation of capital; and they challenge not just economic exploitation but also the patriarchy, racism, colonialism and statism entwined with capitalism. Such cooperatives are the building blocks of what I call an ‘anticapitalist peace’ – a peace not satisfied with the silencing of arms, nor with positive peace that doesn’t challenge capitalist logic, but one that transforms the economic relations at the root of violence. I have encountered two cases that demonstrate this concretely, in two different parts of the world.

In 2014, as Syria was disintegrating under the weight of a brutal civil war, something unusual happened in the country’s north and east. The Kurdish people – after a century of systemic oppression – declared de facto democratic autonomy in the territories they began to control. Instead of declaring a new nation-state, however, they set up a system of assemblies, communes, cantons and cooperatives that sought to reorganise social life from below, under principles of democratic confederalism. This project was formalised as the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria, better known as Rojava.

Everyone debated and made decisions about their neighbourhood, their communities, their families

By the time I arrived in early 2018, the project’s economic architecture – in service of a social economy that prioritised social, ecological and collective goals over profit maximisation – was already in place. I’d come to Rojava for doctoral research but also because it was the first time Kurds were putting democratic confederalism into practice and building cooperatives as part of a revolutionary movement. I wanted to witness that process myself, and to tell the world that an anticapitalist economy was possible. By then, half a million hectares of land had been communalised with collective-use rights, and cooperatives had sprung up in every town. Women’s economic committees are central to Öcalan’s argument that a communal economy should be guided by knowledge preserved by women over the course of capitalism’s development and spread, precisely because women think (or have typically had to think) about collective need and care. They were introducing the model to their communities with the slogan ‘one cooperative for every commune’.

Upon my arrival, what I found most immediately striking was not the scale of the project but the transformation of everyday time. In Rojava, people typically work until 2.30 pm, return home to eat and rest, then go out again at 5 pm – not to work more hours, but to take part in an assembly: of the cooperative, the commune, the women’s congress or the municipality, where everyone debated and made decisions about their neighbourhood, their communities, their families. Almost no one chose to stay at home. This organisation of time was a radical departure from the exhaustion that capitalism imposes seemingly everywhere else, where punishing schedules and precarity systematically prevent people from having any say over their own lives, leaving the state or the market as the only actor capable of making decisions about the collective.

Karl Marx called it alienated labour: work that doesn’t express human capacities but instead exhausts them, that turns both body and time into commodities. This form of violence produces no visible corpses, no headlines, but something essential is destroyed all the same: the possibility of deciding over one’s own life. What do I produce? For whom? How do I want to live? Under capitalism, such questions are answered not by people but by the market. In Rojava, people sought to answer these questions collectively – What do we produce? For whom do we produce? How do we produce? – in assemblies and other public fora, and established cooperatives accordingly.

In the commune assemblies that I attended, people deliberated these questions in relation to electricity, grain and bread. Answering ‘How many loaves will we produce?’ required knowing how many families ate bread and how much bread they typically consumed. But ‘How will we produce it?’ demanded something else entirely: the founding of a bread cooperative that reversed a belief – ‘We are a society that no longer knows how to make bread’ – born of what many considered the Syrian state’s colonial-era ‘prohibition’ on baking one’s own bread. Strictly speaking, no formal prohibition existed; rather, state subsidy programmes and a ration-card system for wheat and flour made people dependent on cheap, state-distributed bread, which undermined the practice of baking at home. To want to return to older methods was to have to relearn them, to recover knowledge that had often been taken away deliberately.

Then there was the question of milk, from a cooperative built to raise animals: should it go to the children first, to the neighbours, or should it become the basis of a yogurt factory? Answers to each had to be found. In other words, as communes debated how to produce to meet their needs, they were never simply weighing inputs against outputs; they were reaching for an economy grounded in anticolonial practice and in an ethical distribution of the surplus. Everyone who lived in the commune took part in these debates – the differences of political opinion, religious belief and ethnic identity that had been named as causes of Syria’s civil war were not, here, a source of conflict or division. They became, instead, the commune’s social wealth, raw material from which richer, more varied answers and solutions could be found.

Equally central to the project was its feminist dimension. Rojava’s social economy is based on a principle that mainstream economics – and most Left movements – have historically ignored: reproductive and care work, performed predominantly by women, is not a secondary complement to the economy, but its foundation. When that work remains invisible and confined to the domestic sphere, women cannot partake in political life and are unable to participate in the assemblies that build autonomy. Rojava’s social economy promoted the socialisation of such work through cooperatives where women could participate without commodifying their labour. Across Kurdistan, for instance, women have always prepared preserves for the turn of the seasons: cheeses, pickled vegetables, dried produce, ground spices. Done alone, for one’s own family, this work was never counted as economic activity, even though it catered to a large share of collective need. These preserves aren’t just food, either: they carry memory, culture, the rhythm of the land’s cycles. The cooperatives built around them safeguard that inherited knowledge and turn it into a shared capacity, allowing women to produce for their families and communities, and exchange or sell the surplus to meet other needs.

I found this to be deeply intuitive: if the organisation of the economy is itself the organisation of life, then transforming the economy ceases to be a distant or abstract struggle, instead becoming a concrete way of inhabiting the world daily. This socialisation is not incidental or complementary to peace; it is a structural condition of peace.

Political autonomy is destroyed by military force; cultural identity is granted as a gesture of tolerance

What I witnessed in Rojava was something I had rarely seen in post-conflict contexts: peace built not as the absence of war – because war continues in Rojava – but as a way of daily life. Historically, millions of people were living a process of true self-governance, with their identities reconstituted and their voices active in collective decision-making. To build anticapitalist peace, Rojava shows, negative peace is not indispensable. The form of social organisation is what matters.

Today, this social organisation is at an inflexion point. At the beginning of 2026, Syrian government forces, jihadist groups and Turkish-backed militias launched a large-scale offensive on Kurdish-administered territories, forcing the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) to withdraw from the Arab territories they had administered for years, falling back to the original Kurdish heartland of Rojava. A ceasefire agreement signed at the end of January required the SDF to formally cede key territories, renounce strategic oil fields, and integrate individually into the Syrian army, without recognition as an autonomous force. For many within the movement, this amounted to capitulation: the surrender of 14 years of revolutionary construction under threat of a war of extermination.

What the Damascus government offered in return was telling: recognition of Kurds as a cultural minority – the right to speak their language, to preserve certain identity expressions – but no autonomous Kurdish-language education system, no constitutional recognition of self-determination, no structure of self-governance whatsoever. Political autonomy is destroyed by military force; cultural identity is granted as a gesture of tolerance. This is the characteristic hypocrisy of state multiculturalism: erasing real power while preserving folklore.

This development does not invalidate what Rojava built – on the contrary, it makes it more urgent to understand. It shows that anticapitalist peace faces not only the direct violence of war, but also the structural violence of the state and the market, which seek to reclaim territories where people organised themselves differently. And it demonstrates that this form of organisation was real enough, threatening enough to the established order, to be deemed worthy of destruction.

Despite the current situation in Rojava, the sense of everyday peace that cooperativism fosters among and within communities that I observed over the course of my fieldwork has led me to reflect more specifically on the role of cooperatives in post-conflict and peacebuilding contexts. In fact, for the past two years, peace negotiations are once again underway between the PKK and the Turkish state; one of my aims in writing this essay is to make the case for cooperatives to be on the agenda for a potential peace agreement. It is in this context that I became interested in the role cooperatives have played in Colombia, following the peace agreement in 2016 between the Colombian government and the FARC-EP, the country’s largest rebel group.

The accord, signed after more than half a century of armed conflict, was described by the Kroc Institute for International Peace Studies at the University of Notre Dame in Indiana as the most comprehensive of the 34 agreements signed worldwide since the end of the Cold War. Among its notable innovations was a proposal for the collective reincorporation of ex-combatants through cooperatives and other associative forms of a social economy.

The project must sustain itself within the capitalist market even as it attempts to transcend it

During negotiations, the FARC-EP had challenged the UN’s classic disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration model. The FARC’s primary argument against this model was that it prioritised individual adaptation to the labour market and that this amounted to accepting the unjust order they had spent decades fighting. Instead, they proposed ‘reincorporation’ – a form of integration that recognised the political agency of signatories and their intention to continue the struggle for social transformation, now through civilian means.

This is how ECOMÚN (Economías Sociales del Común, or Social Economies of the Commons) came to be in 2017: a federation comprising approximately 6,200 peace-agreement signatories and 154 organisations across 26 of Colombia’s 33 administrative divisions. I attended its governing council assembly in 2024. What I found most significant about ECOMÚN was that none of its cooperatives – for coffee, cattle-ranching, fish-farming, textiles, rural tourism, to name a few – were composed exclusively of ex-combatants. Rather, they worked alongside peasant farmers, Indigenous peoples, Afro-Colombians – local communities who share histories of exclusion and dispossession. ‘We have fostered connections between people,’ Juan Camilo Londoño, ECOMÚN’s executive director, told me. ‘There are even organisations that are not signatories but have joined ECOMÚN.’ Internally, the movement describes this as a ‘pedagogy of peace’: the transformation of former war territories into spaces where people on opposing sides of the conflict build productive projects together and, in doing so, weave new social relations.

Yet, as its own leaders acknowledge with clear-eyed honesty, ECOMÚN operates under a fundamental contradiction: the accord did not guarantee the anticapitalist transformation that genuine peace would have required. The question of land tenure – the heart of the FARC’s struggle for decades – was negotiated but never translated into terms that guaranteed real agrarian reform. The project must sustain itself within the capitalist market even as it attempts to transcend it. Its viability depends on volatile political conditions and on international cooperation, which frequently imposes its own neoliberal logics. And because it emerged from the peace agreement, it operates within Colombia’s legal framework and under direct oversight from state agencies. ECOMÚN, in other words, cannot claim Rojava’s autonomy: it is woven into state institutions rather than built in parallel to – or against – them. What self-management it achieves is real, but limited.

What Rojava and ECOMÚN have in common is not their context – one is a revolution in the midst of war; the other is a post-conflict process within a capitalist state – but their wager: that peace is built from below, when people recover control over their time and territories, their cultures and economies.

Both cases also demonstrate that real peace is inseparable from anticolonial and antiracist struggles. For decades, the Kurdish people were denied recognition as an ethnicity, forbidden from speaking their language, and dispossessed of everything that belonged to them: their identity, but also their subsistence economies, their ways of organising themselves, their ways of inhabiting the land. In Rojava, therefore, cooperatives are spaces where the social fabric torn apart by decades of forced assimilation is reconstituted, and where power over one’s own life is recovered. Meanwhile, in Colombia, ECOMÚN’s cooperatives are organised in territories where peasants, Indigenous peoples and Afro-Colombian communities have been, over centuries, systematically dispossessed of their lands. The pedagogy of peace that emerges from these initiatives goes beyond reconciling former enemies – it reconstitutes collective identities that the nation-state and the market had reduced to subalternity, and undoes the manufactured hostility between groups set against each other through systemic poverty and violence.

But it would be a mistake to read these experiences only as responses to extreme situations – as solutions for those living in war zones or conditions of severe poverty. That reading reproduces, perhaps without intending to, the very logic it criticises: the idea that the problem lies over there, in places that have not yet reached capitalist ‘normality’, and that the solution lies in economic development that will better integrate them into the logic of the market.

Peace is not a state reached by signing a document but a way of living together each day

The rhythm of life I observed in Rojava – working until 2.30-3 pm, then going to the assemblies – is precisely what capitalism denies to most people in the world, not just those living in conflict zones. The urban worker who leaves home before dawn and returns at night, too exhausted to speak with their children; the woman whose care work is invisible to the economy and the state, who never rests because her work never ends; the debt-ridden professional who works to pay for what they need to keep working; the young person who sees no horizon in the future; the children who grow up without spaces to play. All of them experience forms of violence that have no name in peace debates but are deeply felt in daily life.

The Guatemalan ex-combatant’s question – What now? – is a question that might be asked not only by someone who survived war but also anyone who works without knowing why, who consumes without feeling satisfied, and who lives with the sense that something essential has been taken from them. Cooperatives are not the only possible answer to that question, but they do propose something that the dominant peacebuilding paradigm – and the economic system that sustains it – systematically refuses to admit: that peace is not a state reached by signing a document but a way of living together each day, of recovering self-determination over one’s own time, needs and relationships, of asking the question How do we want to live? and believing that it can be answered through collective deliberation, by people themselves, without bosses or owners.

This is what the Guatemalan ex-combatant did not find when he came down from the mountains, and what the cooperatives of Rojava and Colombia are trying to build – under very different conditions, with enormous contradictions, but with a clarity about the goal that peace agreements signed in conference rooms rarely possess. Galtung proposed that we dismantle the structures of violence and called what remained ‘positive peace’ – but an anticapitalist peace does not just settle for the absence of structural violence, it dares to ask what should take its place. And it answers with bread baked by hand, milk shared before it is sold, assembly meetings where people still have time and energy to decide. It rests on a form of togetherness in which life itself is harmonious and worth wanting, built each day, from below, through real practice.
