item.title: Traction!
item.dc:creator: Jennifer R Vail
item.description:
Tribologists study friction: what happens when things rub together. It’s indispensable, from the wheel to the paths of stars

- by Jennifer R Vail

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

16 minute listen

In conversations, few words catch my attention faster than ‘friction’ – and especially talk of making things frictionless. From the workplace to grocery shopping, our societies seem to be striving to remove friction from everything. The motivation appears to be that decreasing resistance makes life easier and smoother.

Having spent a career as a tribologist, studying friction, wear and lubrication scientifically, I have some opinions on this. I’ll confess that, in most of my career, I too have sought to reduce friction, developing new materials, designs or even instrumentation in order to lower friction in a jet engine or reduce emissions from your car. However, I’ve also found myself trying to figure out how to increase friction to remove plaque on teeth.

The reality is that friction, despite seeming so antagonistic, is necessary and even productive. The force that resists motion has, since humans first struck a spark from a stone, been the very thing that propels us forward. And this paradox offers a lens through which to reread humanity’s entire technological history.

In order to appreciate all that an understanding of friction has helped us to accomplish, it’s necessary to start at square one and state what friction actually is. We define friction as the force that resists motion, and that means friction is rather ubiquitous. If things are moving, whether they’re sliding around or rolling, there’s friction. Solids, liquids, gases? Doesn’t matter. If there’s movement, friction is there to resist it. Unfortunately, because friction’s job is to resist, we’ve developed an aversion to it as a nuisance. But it’s a very important force, and we’ve thrived by expanding our understanding of it. By the 1960s, after millennia of evolving with friction, we finally accepted that friction is such a critical part of our world that a scientific field of study needed to be devoted to it: tribology.

Tribologists like me study this force in all its forms. Tribology is the science of interacting surfaces in relative motion, concerned with the wear of materials, friction and lubrication. Basically, tribology is the specialisation of things rubbing against each other. You may raise an eyebrow at a field of science focused on this, but when you pause to consider how much motion is going on inside us, around us and throughout the Universe, you can appreciate that tribology is vast. More than anyone, tribologists know the problems friction can cause. But they also know the achievements that have followed as we’ve come to understand resistance better.

Although tribology as a formalised field is relatively modern, friction has long shaped humanity’s technological innovations. For example, consider its pivotal role in people’s journeys from A to B over the centuries. I’m willing to bet that whenever you need to move unwieldy furniture or carry home that giant bag of cat litter, your instinct is to find a cart to help you. Early humans had a similar thought, turning to log rollers to move heavy objects, and coming up with one of our greatest inventions: the wheel. Rolling makes it easier to move objects because it reduces friction between the object and surface you’re moving it against. There are far fewer surface interactions in the process of rolling versus sliding. Plenty can be said about the wheel, including the fact that even in 2026 we can’t seem to agree on the origin of its discovery, but there is zero doubt that it’s a brilliant innovation for dealing with friction. But wheels also need friction: when we exert a force to move a wheel forward, the force between the ground and the wheel – static friction – keeps it from spinning freely, which would result in us going nowhere. Once forward motion begins, the resistance to motion becomes dynamic friction, which is just as important. If you’ve driven on ice, you know the danger of too little friction.

However, if people hadn’t continued improving on these basic principles, even the wheel would be rather inefficient due to friction.

The Vikings’ longships minimised form drag so they could cut through the water quickly

The ancient Romans discovered this in their amphitheatres. Roman chariot races didn’t come without their headaches. Or rather, foot aches. I’m certain the drivers likely complained about their hot feet, caused by friction between the wheels and axle heating up the surrounding parts. In Odes, a collection of lyric poems, the poet Horace described how chariot wheels would glow during racing. Today, scientists know that this glow is from turning the energy of motion into thermal energy. Roman designers eventually figured out that they could temper the problem by putting axungia (animal fat) grease between the wheel and axle. By doing so, they were applying tribological knowledge already exploited by the Sumerians: that fats and oils work more effectively than water as lubrication between surfaces. However, that created a new conundrum: if the grease got hot enough, it risked catching fire. The solution? A coolant. In this case, they splashed water on the chariots, in the ancient equivalent of a pit stop.

While all roads led to Rome, you could say all seas led to the Vikings. They, too, cleverly adapted to the resistance that met them as they journeyed through the oceans. Moving through fluids produces a type of friction known as drag. Even within drag there are subsets. Skin drag is from the friction between the surface of the ship and the water, whereas form drag stems from the shape of the hull as it moves through the water. When they had to transport cargo safely, the Vikings used sturdy ships with wide hulls. This wider hull increased form drag and slowed them down, but the stability provided was more critical. Their famous longships, however, were long and slim, minimising form drag as much as possible so they could cut through the water quickly.

As with all friction scenarios, however, the Vikings found themselves having to balance some competing demands. Faster longships are better, yes, but it was also imperative that the ships not break apart into pieces from the waves. They needed flexibility and strength, while keeping the ships as light as possible to ride higher in the water to reduce drag. To do this, the Vikings used their ‘clinker’ technique of nailing together long planks of wood. The rivets and overlapping planks would increase drag compared with a more polished, smoother design but these individual planks gave the ships the ability to twist and flex to weather storms. If I was on a boat trip in the middle of the ocean, I too would be happy to sacrifice a little bit of drag reduction to avoid capsizing from a rogue wave.

Looking at boats and ships today, it’s clear that we didn’t just accept these Viking designs as the culmination of nautical perfection. Likewise, we aren’t driving around in Roman chariots today. We have since made incredible leaps forward in understanding how to quantify friction and thus design for it, finally approaching friction scientifically. In the 1920s, Chrysler’s head of engineering Carl Breer had the idea to design cars with aerodynamics in mind. Planes seemed to slice seamlessly through the air. Shouldn’t cars do the same? Breer tasked the engineer William Earnshaw to consult with none other than Orville Wright to learn how to design a car in a wind tunnel. The resulting teardrop-shaped Chrysler Airflow was considered a flop, as many disruptive designs can be when they’re just too jarring for taste, but that flop revolutionised how we design cars. Wind-tunnel testing remains a standard today, and friction’s presence is as expected as the air itself.

Tribology testing is routine for the automotive industry today, and there are tribology labs scattered throughout a variety of industries, from medical to food. In these labs, you’ll find instruments designed to measure friction at macro-scales down to the atomic level. My PhD lab at the University of Florida had tribometers measuring friction in force ranges that covered three orders of magnitude. I’ve even worked in a lab that had a tribometer built to test an actual train wheel against a railway. Tribologists are incredibly clever with innovating ways to measure friction, given how persnickety friction is. Friction is dependent on the conditions of the operation – how fast things are moving, how much force they experience, and what temperature and environment they’re in.

Temperature in particular is a fun variable to contend with, because friction itself leads to temperature changes; indeed, frictional heating can be extreme in some cases. Like with Roman chariots, greases can ignite at certain temperatures making it imperative to control friction heating in order to avoid accidentally reaching that temperature. And for applications like jet engines, which get very hot anyway, we have engineered solid materials with low friction to withstand the heat.

When tribologists run into a wall, we develop a new instrument to understand what friction is trying to tell us

You may think tribology is already a niche field, but we have specialisations within it. Mine was solid lubrication, and I worked on developing and testing materials for jet engines and automobiles. In some cases, the conditions of the end use were so aggressive that the steel I was running my material against would experience enough friction heating to completely change the colour of the steel. That’s how you know you’ve reached the extremes in tribology, but those extremes must be met and they obviously are. After all, we have space stations orbiting Earth and landers on Mars.

Which brings us to another critical point about friction’s role in human progress: resistance is a consequence of progress, and its existence is a sign of progression itself. We wouldn’t have the now-robust business of solid lubricants if we had not advanced technologically to design turbine engines, which themselves were the result of us figuring out powered flight. By achieving that, our progress led us to new resistance. I think this is critical to remember anytime we find ourselves confronting unexpected resistance, and it’s something I remind myself of whenever I get halted in my work. I wouldn’t be stumped by this new resistance if I hadn’t managed to advance myself to this position where the resistance exists.

Often when tribologists run into a wall, we find ourselves developing a new instrument to help us understand what friction is trying to tell us. Tribometers have been designed to mimic all of the variables mentioned above, and that alone is quite a feat of human engineering, but now we also couple them with other techniques that allow us to somehow see what is happening while it’s happening. From maps of frictional heating during operation to how friction is influencing cellular movement, instruments and techniques have enabled us to usher friction into a new era to drive us forward, doing more than just finding clever ways to overcome friction. We can harness it as a tool.

In terms of friction, the 20th century can be thought of as the century in which humans accepted the resistance, and established engineering rigour around friction to propel our technological advances forward. Critically, it’s when we formalised how to overcome friction to be more efficient. As a tribologist, however, I’m far more excited about what the 21st century has brought us. Instead of just overcoming friction, we began fully realising how to harness that resistance to bring in a new era of progress. Exhibit A is once again found in our cars, where friction has been deployed as a tool in sustainability. Braking requires friction, so engineers asked: why don’t we use the consequences of that friction to our advantage? The heat from friction in braking is now used to create electricity in regenerative braking in EVs and hybrids. We must continue to use this creative and fresh perspective when dealing with friction, as opposed to always driving towards frictionlessness. Imagine if those engineers had been so fixated on the negatives of friction that they didn’t harness its power.

Using friction as a tool has come to us only as we’ve evolved to understand the depths of friction, including its behaviours and where it may be lurking. We know it is involved in dynamic processes, so let’s use it to control such processes. Yes, we’ve done so for a while with mechanisms like brakes and dampeners, but expanding this beyond machines has really taken hold in recent decades. Now, we’re looking at how friction may be a tool in perhaps the most impressive machine there is: the human body. It’s possible friction may be a lever to help us better model and understand biological processes and, in turn, help in the development of therapeutics. The rate at which a virus ejects from its protein shell or capsid can dictate whether it results in an active infection or instead remains dormant in the cell. If we want to use viruses to intentionally infect and defeat other viruses or bacteria, then controlling the virus’s ejection rate is crucial. Friction is the key to unlocking this possibility. In 2023, researchers found that, by packing the coils of virus DNA in certain ways, they could increase friction during ejection and slow down its rate of ejection.

Every advance we make generates new friction. We solve one problem, and friction presents another

Recently, our knowledge of friction has taken us to even more surprising places, extending even to helping us understand dark matter. The concept of ‘resistance is your reward for progress’ may be best illustrated by the astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar. Despite the fact that established scientists mocked his theories, Chandrasekhar would go on to become a founder of astrophysics, and is the reason we understand the evolution of stars and interstellar dynamics. In the 1930s, he was interested in how the interactions between stars could lead to their collisions. He calculated the timescales of such collisions and realised, though only after publishing, that things weren’t adding up quite right. This led him back to the drawing board, where he spotted there was a resistance present that no one before had identified: dynamical friction. This friction is a gravitationally induced drag that acts on objects as they interact and move through space.

Fast-forward to the 21st century, and dynamical friction has been used as a tool to infer the presence of dark matter. In 2024, researchers in Hong Kong realised that orbital times weren’t matching up with a couple of stars they were studying that were believed to be circling around black holes. They looked at Chandrasekhar’s concept of dynamical friction and wondered what would happen if they incorporated the contribution of friction from the dark matter surrounding the black hole. Voila! Suddenly, the predicted and calculated orbital times of the stars matched with what they were measuring. Friction was present when humanity first started experimenting with fire and the wheel. Now it’s there as we probe the frontiers of our Universe.

We need friction to move. Without its resistance, Earth’s plates would be in constant motion. We could not walk, or drive, or even hold objects. Understanding how to achieve what we want, in a world requiring this resistance, has been essential in our development.

Yet there is a deeper paradox at work, one that William James captured when he wrote that life is built ‘in the self-governing resistance of the ego to the world’. Every advance we make generates new friction. We solve one problem, and friction presents another. We step forward, and new resistance awaits. This is what progress means: that we have moved into territory that demands new understanding.

Roman engineers learned it when their chariot wheels caught fire. Chandrasekhar discovered this when his calculations didn’t add up. And we will continue to encounter resistance as we push forward.

When people speak of a frictionless world, they imagine ease. But ease without resistance is a wheel spinning in place, motion without progress.

item.title: Bhutan: the last place
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
What happened when people in Bhutan, the last country on Earth without television, were allowed to watch it in 1999?

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded: The isolated nation of Bhutan was the last country on Earth without access to television – until 1999. This short documentary from the PBS investigative series Frontline, first aired in 2002, captures the small Buddhist kingdom as the impact of TV began to reverberate. Beaming in images from around the globe, the medium introduced not just a novel form of distraction, but, as one government official puts it, new desires for things the Bhutanese previously didn’t even know existed. As the film explores, this includes everything from emulating professional wrestlers to buying branded clothing. Throughout, the interviewees – including small children, businesspeople and Buddhist monks – seem, at some level, to be aware that this development is at once culturally corrosive, irresistible and, perhaps, inevitable.

item.title: Other people
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Oldfield
item.description:
Disconnection is at the heart of today’s crises. So my husband and I chose a radical and revealing remedy: living communally

- by Elizabeth Oldfield

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

31 minute listen

Earlier this year, I surfaced from sleep to a strange noise, a loud, human singing reverberating through our bedroom ceiling, then a low, almost animal groaning. My husband and I looked at each other. ‘I think Hatty’s in labour,’ he said.

The rest of the day proceeded in the usual way, getting breakfast for our children, dropping them off at school, meetings, emails, booking in the car for an MOT, but these activities were interspersed with opening the door to midwives, making cups of tea for Hatty, and finding towels to drape around the birth pool that had appeared in our living room. Towards evening, our eighth housemate appeared in a rush of fluids. Two ambulance-loads of paramedics stood around like a flock of green and yellow London parakeets, blessedly unrequired. At one point, there were nine medical professionals, seven housemates, two grandparents of the new arrival and a cat in our terraced London house. It didn’t even feel that full, I thought later, as I poured bleach on bloodstained towels and binned a discarded catheter that had been overlooked in a corner.

I am 42, and I did not expect to end up here. Like most of my peers, I was handed a vision of a home worth striving for with far, far fewer people in it and, to begin with, I followed that script. A middle-class 1980s child, I did well at school, moved away from my home county dormitory town for university, and never went back. London, jobs at the BBC, running a think tank all followed. I lived with good friends, and juggled seeing others between our clashing personal schedules. Then people began to pair up and procreate. I met someone, followed suit, and we clawed our way onto the very bottom of the housing ladder. It was a lovely life. A bit relentless, perhaps, a bit lonely around the edges, too, as the schedules got ever harder to tessellate, the work and care burdens heavier. But we had done it. Our little dyad, with dependants, was standing on its own feet, even if something felt decidedly unstable underneath.

More space, more privacy, more control – all are sold as natural, unquestioned goods to be sought in the unconscious script that most of us carry. For the nuclear family, they are tokens of success and maturity, whereas forgoing these ‘goods’ and living with people you are neither shagging nor parenting has an association with low-status, studenty seasons. Not for proper grownups. My husband and I began to feel the strengthening drag of this story. I sometimes saw it in my mind’s eye as a tide, washing young adults from their family homes into temporarily intertwined clusters (largely in cities), then out again, to the suburbs and beyond, in pairs or alone, in search of a garden, a bigger kitchen, storage space for the mountains of stuff we inevitably accumulate. Swept away from each other, everyone further and further apart.

Every policy issue we researched at the think tank led back inexorably to disconnection. It was labelled different things (overconsumption, fraying trust, the corrosion of democracy, crises of loneliness, mental health, care, climate, housing). But a thread linked them all: our inability to bear each other, to share (our stuff, space, skills, and deepest selves) was actively making the world worse. I came across thinkers who shared my intuition that something largely invisible but all-encompassing was getting in the way of our being together as healthier cultures remembered how to do. Some called it individualism or modernity. Others blamed ‘the machine’ of late-stage capitalism. I never settled on a name I liked, but I felt the disquiet of it. Still, all the intelligent analysis and critique never quite seemed to lead to progressive action, but instead to a conservative turn that half-appealed in its communitarianism and rooted localism, but not in its approach to women and ‘outsiders’.

The message seems to be that the price we pay for the freedoms of liberal individualism is loneliness. You can have personal autonomy, privacy and endless choice; you can outsource most of your needs to the market rather than navigate complex non-transactional relationships with other people that tie you into reciprocity; you can optimise your surroundings, appearance and experiences to your exact preferences, but what gets bundled in for good measure is a sense of existential weightlessness.

I rebelled. Surely there was something between atomisation – what the philosopher Charles Taylor calls the ‘buffered self’ – and hierarchical, authoritarian community; between girl-boss and trad-wife. The final push to try and find it, ultimately, was fear. When my first child was born, the reality of the climate crisis moved from a theoretical policy problem to one that bubbled acidly in my belly, settled itself in my bones. I had brought this powerless being into a world on fire, and the idea that hard work and individual accumulation could keep her safe stopped making sense. The need to be part of a thick web of humans who would not play a passing role in each other’s lives but commit to costly mutual care felt urgent as the ground bucked and roiled beneath our feet. I wanted ‘a village’, as we say now, not for the golden Instagram images of laughing friends around a photogenic table, but because, in my bleakest moments, I thought it might be essential for survival.

It is a truism that early parenthood is isolating and relentless, but does it have to be? We started questioning accepted norms, not idly fantasising about building a commune but taking serious steps. I wanted to live this season of our lives up close with others, witnessing each other, supporting each other. Not uploading the tidied-up details into group chats, after the fact, or smoothing the misery into memes, holding back the joys for fear of sounding smug. This realisation cracked outwards, connecting with a deeper intuition: I wanted all of life to be like that. I wanted to see and be seen. It felt wrong that everyone didn’t live this way, like something important had been lost in the rush to accumulate stuff and protect our security, status and autonomy by disappearing behind our own front doors.

Whether you call the present a polycrisis or just a gigantic roiling clusterfuck, I became more convinced that the medicine for most of our ills is to actively and counterculturally move towards other people. To resist the powerful forces driving us apart. There are lots of ways of doing this, of course. But letting go of the idea that our homes must be private retreats from other people seemed a decent place to start. I believe that our homes can be places to relearn the habits of reciprocity, sharing and mutual care that for most of history (and, in many parts of the non-Western world, still) are the defining characteristics of a culture worthy of the name. A culture we are urgently going to need.

This sounds much, much simpler and easier than it is.

For us, it took years of intentional conversations, initial enthusiasm from others that then petered out, bureaucratic wrangling, and research. We eventually found people who were equally committed (who were not, interestingly, friends already), and rented together to test it. We learned to navigate sex noises and bathroom smells (sound-proofing and background music helps a lot with the first). We had tense conversations about kitchen storage, our different expectations around spending and cleanliness. It surfaced stuff from our childhoods, which we then had to be honest about and confront. The process (much of which happened during COVID-19 lockdowns, which I’m sure accelerated it) was challenging and exposing, almost unbearably uncomfortable at times.

As I held him at 4 am, my son asked: ‘Why couldn’t we stay in our flat, just us?’

We also practised rupture and repair, realising that, even as we saw the most ridiculous, fragile, defensive parts of each other, we were not running away. In his play The Real Thing (1982), Tom Stoppard aptly defined love as ‘Knowledge of each other … knowledge of self, the real him, the real her, in extremis, the mask slipped from the face.’ In the course of our building trust, it did feel a lot like love. Not love based on surface similarities or romance, but on a mutual commitment to each other. It felt like growing up. The existential emptiness, the unsteady sense of vertigo eased.

Having tested the concept, we embarked on a labyrinthically complex joint house-purchase. It fell through on the day of a long-delayed exchange, after we’d reached the end of the notice period on our rental. For months, we had no fixed address and scattered to the sofas and spare beds of friends and family. My youngest child began having nightmares. As I held him at 4 am, he asked: ‘Why couldn’t we stay in our flat, just us?’ The script glowed temptingly. If living with others was the answer, surely it shouldn’t be this difficult. We held our nerve.

To date, we have lived up close – bodily fluids close – with people we are not related to for nearly six years. We share all the space in our jointly mortgaged home except the bedrooms. We pool most of our money, cook, shop, pray and host hundreds of guests a year, together. And we manage countless petty conflicts, over the milk or the dishwasher or the crumbs on the side, conflicts that often mask deeper questions: who do I belong to? Where can I be really at home, be really myself? Who am I becoming, alongside these people? And are we able, when it comes down to it, to be each other’s safety?

There are very few models for what we are doing. Perhaps the most robust is the monastic tradition. Most orders of religious Sisters or Brothers see the proximity of living up close with each other as essential to spiritual growth. It is precisely in the discomfort of being witnessed, up close, at our worst, in being asked to compromise preferences, to share and serve others, they argue, that we really grow up.

Living with others has shown me things in myself that I would prefer to ignore

My policy-wonk brain knew there were systems keeping us apart. Not just social scripts but monetary policies, mortgage terms, HMO (house in multiple occupation) legislation. Yet living communally has taught me that it is also what is inside us that makes it hard to be together. My romantic ideas about cultures worthy of the name, marked by interdependence and mutual care, clearly also require certain kinds of people – with emotional skills, developed character, an ability to make lasting commitments. None of which my individualistic formation had gifted me an abundance of.

Living with others has shown me things in myself that I would prefer to ignore. How much of me is still a child, wanting my way, quick to cry ‘it’s not fair’. I have been learning all this as the world around us unravels. The contrast is disconcerting. If it really is the end of the world, at least as we have known it, then what kind of people will be needed? What would it take to be braver, more resilient and flexible, more joyful, creative and free? A person who could, at bloody least, wait patiently to go in the bathroom, or let someone else use a favourite mug. Someone able to sacrifice sleep to care for another’s child, and have the hard conversation about a failure to mop the kitchen floor, rather than avoiding it. I want to learn these habits. I have a hunch that much more than this might be asked of me. Of all of us.

This project finds faint echoes in the self-improvement, self-development, self-optimisation we are all constantly hectored into – therapy (or psychedelics, or stoicism) for the mind and Hyrox (or reformer Pilates, or yoga) for the body (with those who are not working on themselves in some way being the exception). Interestingly, the unconventional way our household lives is rarely recommended to those seeking self-knowledge or self-development. The standard advice is an inward turn in order to facilitate a private excavation of an authentic self, along with strong personal boundaries that draw distinct lines between that self and others. Porousness tends to be framed as deleterious to Project Self. Most monastic orders encourage periods of solitude and silence, to be sure, but much of daily life is spent in an exposing proximity to others, the very idea of which would bring most of us out in hives.

This difficult proximity, where we witness and are witnessed without our protective, polished personas is an immensely powerful change agent. You can see it in action in group therapy, the recovery movement and some short-term intensive self-development programmes, but this powerful ‘technology of the self’, to use Michel Foucault’s phrase, is vanishingly rare. This kind of witnessing (during my housemate’s labour, for example, I witnessed parts of her that only her partner otherwise sees) is effective because change requires us to be honest about who we currently are. Living in community is where illusions about the self go to die!

One of the phrases we use a lot in our household is ‘We are made for each other and we are made by each other.’ Marxists such as Silvia Federici call this ‘social reproduction’. Neurologically, this makes sense: human interaction shapes our brains from our very earliest moments. Every human comes into the world in search of a gaze.

The day the baby was born, while their mother was being stitched up and I was moving bins for the paramedics, my primary-school aged son was one of the first people to hold the tiny form. They’d wrapped the baby in a yellow foil survival bag, and he gazed down for long minutes with as much attention as if he was indeed holding a giant Quality Street toffee. This baby had moved from deep bodily entanglement, hidden in just one of us, to a less visible but no less profound interdependence. They have now been held by more arms than your average Western infant, and whether it’s mum, dad, us housemates, family, neighbours or church friends, we all adopt the same posture as my son. Face turned towards face. Eyes meeting eyes. The baby makes noises, and we make noises back. And as we gaze and gurgle, the mycelia of their brain are forming.

Dan Siegel, the clinical psychiatrist and founder of interpersonal neurobiology, says that our earliest relationships ‘shape the very neural structures that create representations of experience and allow a coherent view of the world: Interpersonal experiences directly influence how we mentally construct reality.’ The connections formed by the face-dancing we all instinctively do with babies help create the conditions that enable them to experience what is real. More than this, these gazes are where their sense of self comes from. Siegel says that, beyond these earliest experiences of connection, relationships shape, throughout our lives, ‘how we feel, how we think, how we remember things, how we tell the story of who we are, the sense of self … what gives you a sense of purpose.’ We become who we become because of who we gaze on, and who gazes back at us.

We talk a lot about exits, about the fact that we will probably not live together forever

The porousness of babies to their caregivers, and especially their need for face-to-face connection is widely understood. The neuropsychologist Allan Schore calls a baby an ‘open dynamic system’. What our house is helping me see is how much humans remain ‘open systems’, and how much mind/self/soul (all translations of the word ‘psyche’) arises within and between us. We are not closed selves, semaphoring information to each other and making free rational choices. We are always makers of each other – the act of mutual witnessing, or its lack, moulding us like wet clay.

One way of thinking about our unconventional living situation, then, is that it offers a way of choosing who we want to be formed by, as if consciously curating the powerful gaze of others. Our bet is that the real costs, in control, convenience and comfort, the exposure of being seen and known ‘with masks slipped from faces’, are worth it. I believe that it is a demanding but effective method of becoming the kind of people the world needs now.

I could be wrong. I am not rosy-tinted about the realities of experiments like these, how badly they can hurt people if done poorly. The way we live may not last. We commit, unlike monks and nuns, only in five-year increments. This season has been the most meaningful, the most beautiful and the most fun of my life, despite the challenges. It has made me braver, and freed up swathes of time and energy that I would have otherwise spent on home admin in a household of only two adults. It is working, really working, for now, but we are realists. We talk a lot about exits, about the fact that we will probably not live together forever. Perhaps we’re trying to have our cake and eat it, keeping one foot in the autonomy of liberal individualism even as we experience the benefits of rooted, committed mutual care. Our experiment is imperfect. My hunch, though, is that we are going to need more of them.

As a society, we are still largely in denial about the scale of the existential threats facing us, and against which individualism cannot keep us safe. In times of deep ecological, technological and political crisis, we may be forced to remember how to be each other’s safety. To unpick, laboriously, the conditioning of the weird, prosperous West and call bullshit on the lie that control, accumulation and a frictionless, precision-optimised life was ever going to make us happy. Though I know it’s a lie, a lot of me still wants it. However, as I learn every day how deeply the script of individualism has formed me, I also see how poorly it serves us.

Each day that I wake up in this house, I am choosing to enact a different script, one in which other people’s concerns are more real to me. My housemate’s labour pains, this baby’s cries, are my business. Conversely, my occasional existential terror or my children’s school struggles are tangible to a wider group of people than they would otherwise be. We have a stake in each other. There is a fierce tenderness in it that often brings me to tears. Iris Murdoch describes something like it in ‘The Sublime and The Good’ (1959) when she writes:

Love is the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real. Love … is the discovery of reality … The exercise of overcoming one’s self, of the expulsion of fantasy and convention … is indeed exhilarating. It is also, if we perform it properly which we hardly ever do, painful.

Isolation allows us to maintain all kinds of illusions about ourselves and about others. In contrast, remaining tethered to a shared reality requires us to really see others, not in the refracted fun-house mirror of social media, but in regular, embodied ways. We triangulate the world via other people, taking readings from a range of perspectives to build a more accurate picture of things. My image of this process is of humans echolocating like bats, where the objects sounding back are the voices and faces of other people. René Descartes might have thought he needed to withdraw from society completely to find truth but, respectfully, he was wrong. Turning in, pulling away disorientates us. The social theorist Sarah Stein Lubrano argues that the more time we spend alone, the more prone we are to delusion. Communities like ours are often laughed at, written off as naive, but if our minds do indeed require a thick web of strong relational connections in order to grasp reality, then we weirdos are possibly learning to see the world more clearly.

Our community (and other lasting ones) hold together by turning attention beyond ourselves

Why, then, are experiments like ours so rare? Why do I, a public advocate, a recipient of the very real benefits of communal living, still feel conflicted about arguing more strongly for it to become the norm? It is partly that such a life is, as Murdoch says, painful. Decentering my preferences, letting go of my self-aggrandising illusions hurts. These are growing pains, every one worth it – but still. Inviting others into something this rigorous, and costly, is not in fashion.

There is another reason. The community we live in offers mutual witnessing, mutual recognition, increased capacity and care, and economies of scale, but this alone is not enough to hold us when it all feels too much. When people come to our home wanting advice about setting up something similar, we always tell them: community for the sake of community doesn’t work. Communes might be highly effective sites of self-formation, but the ones designed primarily to do that will likely collapse. My experience is that our community (and other lasting ones) hold together by turning attention beyond ourselves. The ability to locate the project in a vision of the good – political, ecological, philosophical or other – is an essential foundation.

There is something about our house I have not mentioned much. You may have caught that throwaway line about praying together. One of the arguments made by Charles Taylor and others about the isolating tendencies of modernity is that it is linked to secularity. He argues that pre-moderns had a much stronger sense of how porous they were, how bound up with each other, with nature, and with divine or magical presences. He links our increasingly boundaried or buffered sense of self to the loss of religion: we moderns are not made by and for god(s), by and for each other, but by and for ourselves. I have some sympathy with the argument, because without a robust, collective wisdom tradition, it is challenging to keep choosing to move towards each other. Despite believing in this way of life for policy reasons, emotional reasons, neurobiological reasons, even goddamn survival reasons, I am not sure I would be able to do it without a powerful, and in our case, religious, reason why.

When asked to sum up his teaching, Jesus offered two, interlinked commands. Firstly, love of the divine (Love the Lord your God ‘with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength’) then, love of the other (‘Love your neighbour as yourself’). No moral prescriptions or religious ritualism, but relationality as The Way. I have spent a lot of time sitting with the work that the word ‘as’ is doing in ‘love your neighbour as your self’. In the same measure you love yourself? At the same time as? Because they are yourself? Even when they have left beard clippings all over the sink?

The petty squabbles between early believers trying to share are there in the New Testament for all to see

Helpfully, Jesus had a lot of other less cryptic things to say about learning to bear each other and be together. The New Testament takes it as a given that humans are messy, dishonest, selfish, misguided, that we will hurt and anger each other. We may be made for and by each other, but it assumes there will be days when we wish we were not. This tendency to disconnect, this almost gravitational pulling away from each other led Martin Luther, building on Augustine, to call us ‘Homo incurvatus in se’: humanity turned in on itself. I find it one of the more useful definitions of sin.

The New Testament is largely a set of letters between what we might see as communitarian experiments, and reckoning with our inward-turning tendencies. The petty squabbles between early believers trying to share their lives and possessions are there on the page for all to see. The difficulty was part of the point, not a reason to avoid it.

This realism might be why, despite its very real benefits, this is not a full-throated advertisement for communal life. The costs are real, so you need a powerful story to hold you. A completely different script of what a good life looks like. I don’t think it necessarily has to be a religious one, but it does need to be powerful, and go beyond individual interest. Setting up my life for mutual care and reciprocity is the best thing I have ever done, but its chafing against the script I was born into still leaves blisters sometimes. On days when it asks more of me than I am receiving, it is the ‘why’ that makes me stay.

I hope that, collectively, we can (re)discover some big whys, that more people are inspired to experiment with moving towards each other. I think the upending of the world by climate change, AI and all their currently unforeseen effects will likely force us into it. It is, ultimately, soul work. Our household has had a few years’ head start, no more than a foundation course, yet it is getting easier as the vestiges of the old script become threadbare. I think – I hope? – that I am more patient and less petty; more steady and less resistant to sharing. More oriented towards a rigorous love, and so a tiny bit more of use in this hurting world. Whether that is in fact reality or self-delusion is a question you would have to ask my housemates.

item.title: When it started to burn
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
Horrific violence, enduring terror and ceaseless solidarity: four years of war through the eyes of Ukrainian civilians

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
The Norwegian filmmaker Anders Hammer is known for short films that capture global conflicts on the ground as they unfold. These include Do Not Split (2020), which follows the pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong, and The Takeover (2023), which chronicles the lives of Afghan women in the wake of the Taliban’s return to power.

The third film in this trilogy, When It Started to Burn, documents Russia’s invasion of Ukraine over the course of four years, beginning in March 2022, as a combination of deep uncertainty and extraordinary resolve was setting in across the country. In particular, the film follows the life of a Kyiv native named Kseniia, who makes the difficult decision to send her children abroad as she stays in the country and runs a ‘humanitarian headquarters’ distributing donations to those in need. Through his portrait of the invasion from the perspective of Ukrainian civilians, Hammer explores how their lives are defined by horrific violence, enduring terror and ceaseless solidarity.

item.title: How intuitions work
item.dc:creator: Marc A Moffett
item.description:
Just as seeing a tree gives you reason to believe it’s there, sensing that a stranger is creepy gives you reason to walk away

- by Marc A Moffett

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

29 minute listen

‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
‘This seems like phishing. I wouldn’t click that link.’
‘Something about this deal feels off. Walk away.’

When people say such things, they are not typically drawing conclusions from a chain of reasoning. The person who avoids getting in the stranger’s car is not thinking: ‘He displayed these three behavioural cues and, therefore, he poses a risk.’ The email isn’t flagged by going through an explicit checklist. The deal doesn’t announce its flaws through a formal audit. In each case, something is simply presented as having a certain character: the man as creepy, the email as fraudulent, the deal as suspect. And yet, acting on these intuitions seems not merely excusable but entirely reasonable. If the man really does strike you as creepy, staying out of his car was probably the smart call – even if you can’t say why.

Despite this, ‘vibes’ and ‘intuitions’ are often dismissed both in daily life and in academic enquiry as irrational or merely heuristic devices. And while we cannot always trust such reactions, they are central, indeed indispensable, to our ability to rationally navigate the world. Philosophers, however, have done surprisingly little to illuminate the rational credentials of these ordinary kinds of intuitions. Instead, they have focused the bulk of their attention on a much more rarefied kind of intuition called rational intuition, which is taken to function primarily in the a priori disciplines of philosophy, logic and mathematics.

My objective is to explain why our everyday intuitive reactions can have such rational force. The key is to see that intuition works in much the same way as perception, in that both can directly present something to us as actual. Once we understand what gives perception this feature, we can see why intuitions might involve exercising the same basic kind of cognitive capacity.

A standard way of characterising rational intuition is in terms of seemings, by analogy with perception. Just as it perceptually seems to you that there is a car in the garage, so it can intellectually seem to you that 2 + 2 = 4 – the former presenting a physical fact, the latter a conceptual one. But rational intuition and the everyday intuition at work when you decline to get in a stranger’s car are not as far apart as this rarefied example suggests: the philosopher’s intuition is, at bottom, a highly specialised version of the same basic capacity.

To draw these two capacities together, let’s consider a favourite pastime of philosophers: the thought experiment. Philosophers have a penchant for exotica, which is never more clearly on display than in their invocation of thought experiments. Consider two cases that have occupied philosophers for decades – one from ethics, one from the theory of knowledge.

In the trolley problem, the philosophers Philippa Foot and Judith Jarvis Thomson imagined a runaway trolley hurtling toward five people tied to the track. You are standing on a bridge above, next to another bystander. The only way to stop the trolley and save the five is to push the bystander off the bridge. If you do, his body will halt the trolley, but he will die as a result. Many people feel, immediately and forcefully, that pushing him is wrong, even if it saves five lives. But why?

We routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life

Or consider Carl Ginet’s case involving fake barns. Imagine you are driving through the countryside and see a barn. It looks exactly like a barn; you’re paying attention, the light is good. You form the perfectly reasonable belief that this is a barn. What you don’t know is that you’re in ‘fake-barn country’: the region is dotted with elaborate barn facades, indistinguishable from real barns when viewed from the road. You happen to be looking at the one real barn in this area. Your belief is true, and it seems justified. And yet almost everyone who considers this case has the immediate, firm sense that you don’t really know it’s a barn. But why not?

To sceptics and the uninitiated, these thought experiments can seem fantastical. Because we encounter them in their most dramatic forms, like runaway trolleys and fake barns, thought experiments seem exotic. But properly understood, these imaginative episodes are important tools for sharpening our grasp of key concepts. In fact, their functioning is continuous with something far more familiar: the way we routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life, wondering what might happen if we take one path rather than another in the proverbial fork in the road.

These imaginings are just thought experiments as they appear in everyday life. Imagine you are deciding whether to tell a friend that his husband has been unfaithful. You picture the conversation, the shock, the hurt that registers on his face. And in that imagined moment, you see that causing such pain is a reason to hold your tongue, even if it’s not a good or decisive one.

How did you determine that this was a reason against divulging the infidelity? It’s not as if you literally see that causing pain is a reason not to do something, nor do you infer it from other things. Rather, in entertaining the possibility, you apprehended his pain as a relevant consideration, as something that counts against disclosure. Its status as a reason emerged not from an argument, but directly from your understanding. It just seems like a reason to hold your tongue.

Intuition’s verdicts simply present themselves, with no organ at work

Notice that this phenomenon also occurs in the thought experiments discussed above. It just seems wrong to push the bystander from the bridge; similarly, it just seems false that you would know it was a real barn in fake-barn country. In both cases, the answer doesn’t arise from an argument. These intuitions arrive unbidden, prior to any deliberation.

These seemings have an unmistakable epistemic pull. Because your friend’s pain seems like a reason, we accept it as such: the seeming is the reason. What is striking is not simply that we have such seemings, but that we trust them. They are involved in shaping our deliberations, guiding our actions, and eliciting belief. They do not merely occur to us; they appear to reveal something about how things must be in the imagined scenario.

For all their ordinariness, however, intuitions remain puzzling. In perceptual experience, we at least have an established framework: the world impinges on our senses, and different perceptual modalities reinforce one another. In the end, we can trace the causal route it takes to produce them. Intuition offers no such apparatus. Its verdicts simply present themselves, with no organ at work and nothing we can point to that they make contact with. Consequently, we rely on them without a clear account of their nature or epistemic authority. But before we can understand intuitions themselves, we need to situate them within a broader epistemological landscape, one shaped by attempts to unify the justification of our basic beliefs.

We all have beliefs about the world, and we care whether they are true. We want to get things right. But we can’t step outside our own minds to check a belief against the world; the best we can do is to hold it for good reasons – for considerations that, from where we stand, speak in favour of its truth. That is what justification is.

Now suppose that beliefs could only ever be justified by other beliefs. Then, as the ancient Sceptics observed, no belief could ever be justified at all. Each belief would derive its support from further beliefs, which would themselves require further support, and so on without end. To foil this regress, we have three options: embrace an infinite chain (infinitism), allow the chain to loop back on itself (coherentism), or hold that some beliefs are justified independently of others (foundationalism). It is this final option, the view that there is a starting point or foundation for justification, that I will develop. But to do so, we must spend a little time explaining how a belief can be justified by something other than another belief.

If it visually seems to you that there is a tree, then you have a justification for believing that there is a tree

Perception is the simplest example. When I see a tree, my visual experience makes it seem as if there is a tree in front of me. I am presented with the tree. As the philosopher William Tolhurst once put it, perceptual seemings have ‘the feel of truth’, a sense of revealing how things really are (unlike mere thoughts, imaginings or desires, which lack this air of disclosure). But visual experiences are not themselves beliefs: I can have them without forming a belief, perhaps because I distrust my eyesight or suspect my drink has been spiked. Conversely, I can believe there is a tree without seeing it, perhaps because I am told there is one there. Nevertheless, the fact that my visual experience seems to reveal a tree to me is relevant to explaining why I come to believe there is one and why this belief is reasonable.

This is the set-up we need in order to stop the regress of reasons: a state – the visual experience – that is not a belief, but that can nevertheless justify my belief. One influential proposal, developed in different ways by Jim Pryor and Michael Huemer, is that when the world seems to us to be a certain way, we thereby have some justification for believing that it is that way – unless we have a reason to distrust it. More specifically, if it visually seems to you that there is a tree in front of you, then you simply have a justification for believing that there is a tree. The justification does not depend on possessing independent reasons to think that your perceptual system is functioning properly, or that you are not hallucinating, or that your environment is benign. The perceptual seeming itself carries justificatory weight. Of course, my justification can be defeated (for instance, by evidence that I have taken a hallucinogen). The point is simply that no further positive belief is needed for a perceptual seeming to rationally support the corresponding belief.

This provides the basic framework for solving the regress problem. Perceptual experiences are not themselves beliefs, yet they provide reasons for belief. And they do so without relying on antecedent justified beliefs and are not themselves in need of justification. Still, this leaves us with an important question: what is it about these experiences that allows them to justify belief in this way?

Perceptual experience in general, and visual experience in particular, have two familiar features. First, as we have seen, they seem to reveal the world to us, to present objects and properties as actually being out there in the world. Second, they have a vivid phenomenology, a distinctive what-it’s-likeness, as the philosopher Thomas Nagel put it. Many philosophers take these two features to be inseparable: perception seems to disclose reality because it feels the way it does. On this standard view, its phenomenology is presentational, and it is this presentational phenomenology that explains the epistemic force of perceptual experience.

It is at this point that intuitions re-enter the story. According to John Bengson’s concept of quasi-perceptualism, we should model the epistemic behaviour of intuitions on the epistemic behaviour of perceptual experiences: if perceptual seemings justify because they possess a presentational phenomenology, and if intuitions are to justify in the same basic way, then they must share that same kind of presentational phenomenology. When we have an intuition, it justifies a corresponding belief by virtue of exhibiting a felt quality analogous to the what-it’s-likeness of perception, a kind of intellectual seeming that presents its content as actual. For instance, think again of the stranger who gives you a seriously creepy vibe. Just as the tree visually seems green, so the stranger may simply seem untrustworthy. Something about him presents itself to you that way without you having worked out what exactly is making you uncomfortable.

On this view, the explanation for the epistemic force of intuition mirrors the explanation for the epistemic force of perception. Both states present certain facts as real (or present certain propositions as true) by virtue of a distinctive presentational phenomenology. Call this the phenomenal strategy. The difference between them lies simply in the character of this phenomenology. In perception, it is an empirical sensory experience of the external world; in intuition, it is an intellectual or conceptual experience that purportedly reveals the normative, modal or conceptual structure of the world. These are features of the world that we comprehend but can’t see – that gratuitous cruelty counts against taking an action (normative structure), that there could be no round square (modal structure), or that the lucky believer in fake-barn country still doesn’t really know (conceptual structure).

A state can feel exactly like perception while failing to present its contents as actual

But this phenomenological theory of the epistemic significance of intuitions faces a serious difficulty, one pressed most forcefully by Timothy Williamson and Ernest Sosa. Many reflective people report that they do not experience anything like the intellectual phenomenology that quasi-perceptualism posits. For them, judging that a proposition ‘seems right’ involves no distinctive experiential quality at all. If intuition lacks the requisite phenomenology in these cases, then the quasi-perceptualist explanation of its epistemic force collapses. (It’s worth evaluating this in yourself: do you feel an experiential quality when evaluating the thought experiments?)

This is the so-called absent intuition challenge. The kind of robust, presentational phenomenology developed on the basis of quasi-perceptualism is something many people simply deny having. Consequently, either these individuals lack introspective access to their own intuitions (an uncharitable conclusion), or the epistemic force of intuition cannot depend on the presence of a special intellectual phenomenology. If intuitions are to justify in the way quasi-perceptualism claims, then something other than phenomenology must be doing the epistemic work.

This conclusion can be pushed further to call into question even the epistemic significance of phenomenology for perception. To see why, consider the phenomenon known as derealisation disorder. Individuals with this condition report that their perceptual experiences feel perfectly normal from the inside – the colours, shapes and sensory qualities are all intact – yet the world does not seem real to them. Their experiences lack any sense of disclosure or revelatory force. In this respect, derealisation is the mirror image of a perfect hallucination. In derealisation, the experience gets things right, but it doesn’t feel like anything is being revealed; in hallucination, the experience gets things wrong, yet it feels totally convincing. The implication is striking. Call this apparent disclosure of reality presentationality: a mental state is presentational when its content is apprehended as how things actually are, rather than merely as they are thought about or imagined. Derealisation shows that neither the information carried by a perceptual state nor the way that state feels are sufficient for presentationality. A state can feel exactly like perception while failing to present its contents as actual. Phenomenology, then, cannot explain the epistemic force of perceptual seemings, let alone intuitions.

This suggests that defenders of quasi-perceptualism have been looking in the wrong place. Earlier, I noted that perceptual experience has two salient features: it has a rich phenomenology, and it seems to reveal the world to us. The phenomenal strategy seized on the first feature – understandably, given how vivid and conspicuous perceptual phenomenology is – and then treated it as the source of the second. But derealisation cases show that phenomenology can remain intact even when the experience loses its revelatory character. What matters for justification is not how we experience something, but how we apprehend it. On the view I defend, presentationality is a cognitive posture, a way of apprehending a content rather than a distinctive way the experience feels. And it is this posture, this way of grasping the world and not its phenomenological glow, that supplies perceptual experience with its epistemic force.

To see what this posture amounts to, it helps to contrast it with more widely discussed attitudes. Belief, for example, is assertive: it commits us to the truth of its content. Imagination, by contrast, is non-assertive: it entertains possibilities without treating them as actual. Presentational attitudes (that is, seemings) occupy a middle ground. This cognitive posture is what makes a seeming capable of justifying a belief: it presents reality without committing to it, offering us a direct but defeasible route to acceptance.

Once we understand presentationality in this way, the case of intuition falls naturally into place. A crucial feature of presentational states is that they are happenings, not actions. They occur in us; we do not perform them. So, when something intuitively seems true, we do not decide to have this intuition any more than we decide to see a tree. It arrives unbidden. This passivity is precisely what allows a seeming to present its content as actual. When an intuition strikes us, we are not making a judgment or forming a belief. We are apprehending the content as the way things are. The intuition presents the scenario as actual in a manner that calls for belief. In this respect, intuitive seemings share the same role as perceptual seemings.

Belief-formation is less like drawing a conclusion and more like yielding to a disclosure

Understood in this way, the absent-intuition challenge dissolves. The quasi-perceptualist assumed that intuition’s presentational force must arise from an intellectual phenomenology analogous to the sensory phenomenology of perception. But if presentationality is a cognitive posture rather than a phenomenological glow, then no special ‘intellectual experience’ is needed. A person may have no distinctive phenomenology when an intuition arises and yet still apprehend the content as actual in the relevant sense. And once a content is apprehended as actual, it is reasonable to form the corresponding belief. The quasi-perceptualist is right that intuition and perception share something fundamental, but wrong about what that shared feature is. It is not a proprietary phenomenology, but the nature of the apprehension itself.

Why should apprehending a content as actual have any epistemic significance? The answer, I think, is simple. Presentational states are the cognitive events that place us in contact with the world or, more precisely, that seem to place us in contact with the world. When something presents itself to us as being the case, our default cognitive response is to form the corresponding belief. When I turn the corner of a building and my eyes fall on a tree, the tree is simply there before me. Believing that there is a tree is not normally a conclusion I draw; rather I simply accept what my experience presents to me. This is not a matter of inference or deliberation; it is the natural way a rational mind responds to what it takes to be reality.

Belief-formation is less like drawing a conclusion and more like yielding to a disclosure. When the apprehension is accurate, this default response reliably produces true belief; when it is not, the response is still intelligible and reasonable. Presentational states are epistemically respectable because they are where the world shows up for us: the point at which reality makes its first claim on belief. Intuitions inherit this status. They are simply the presentational events through which we apprehend the conceptual structure of a situation as actual, and in doing so provide a rational basis for belief without the need for any further epistemic mechanism.

Intuition saturates our ordinary reasoning. Whenever we see what follows from something, notice that something counts in favour of some action, or recognise something as a possible course of action, we are relying on intuition. These moments rarely announce themselves. They do not arrive with phenomenological fanfare. They are woven into the background of our deliberation, operating quietly whenever we take in a situation and immediately apprehend its normative or conceptual contours.

In this sense, intuition is to cognition what perception is to our engagement with the physical world. Perception allows us to navigate our environment by revealing how things stand around us; intuition allows us to navigate the space of reasons, norms and possibilities by revealing how things stand within the conceptual landscape. When we deliberate, we constantly rely on intuitions to apprehend which considerations matter, how they bear on one another, and what follows from them. Intuition is the cognitive means by which the conceptual structure of a situation is revealed to us.

Seen in this light, the thought experiments with which we started no longer appear as philosophical curiosities. They are simply highly controlled instances of a capacity we rely on constantly. When we imagine a runaway trolley or a real barn surrounded by fakes, we are not invoking a mysterious faculty or peering into a metaphysical telescope. We are exercising the same basic capacity we use when we imagine telling a difficult truth to a friend or weigh up different possible courses of action. The only difference is that philosophical cases are crafted to isolate a specific conceptual relation. Their dramatic trappings obscure the fact that they depend on the same presentational attitude at work in more mundane reasoning.

Intuition does not compete with concept application. It enables it

This brings thought experiments back down to earth. Their epistemic significance arises not from exotic subject matter or imaginary scenarios, but from the fact that they trigger intuitions that disclose how certain concepts hang together. To see what it means for concepts to ‘hang together’, consider a familiar principle of storytelling: show, don’t tell. When J R R Tolkien in The Lord of the Rings (1954-55) describes the creature Gollum leading Frodo into the spider Shelob’s lair, he needn’t pause to explain: ‘This is an act of betrayal.’ The narrator doesn’t mark the moment when Gollum’s loyalties shift, or when his intentions cross a moral threshold. We grasp it directly from the unfolding of events. The situation presents itself as a betrayal: the actions, motives and dangers align in a way that demands the application of the concept. That is what I mean when I say that intuitions reveal how concepts hang together. They disclose the otherwise unstated conceptual requirements of a situation.

Now, a sceptic might argue that what is doing the work here is not intuition, but simply our skill at applying concepts. On this view, we respond correctly to cases because we are good at classifying situations. But this misses something crucial about the rationality of these classifications. To apply a concept is to act; it is to make a classificatory judgment. And judgments of this sort are not self-justifying. Simply deciding, without any basis, that a character has betrayed a friend would be epistemically arbitrary. Such judgments must themselves be grounded in something. Intuitions occur in us prior to and independently of any judgment. When a scenario strikes us as a clear instance of betrayal, that intuitive seeming is not itself an act of concept application. It is the pre-judgmental apprehension that makes the resulting judgment (the resulting application of the concept of betrayal) reasonable. In this sense, intuition does not compete with concept application. It enables it.

This same phenomenon of intuitive apprehension preceding judgment also shows up in ordinary perception. When we open our eyes, the world does not appear as a mosaic of colours and shapes. It appears as a scene populated with meaningful objects: a child reaching for a toy, a cat waiting expectantly for dinner, a car approaching too fast. As P F Strawson observed, if we try to describe what we see using only low-level sensory terms (patches of colour, shifting brightness), we falsify the experience. The world comes to us in perception already organised by concepts. What is presented is not bare visual data but things of certain kinds, situated in relations to one another.

And here, intuition enters even into everyday perceptual experience itself. Perception reveals not merely visual arrays but robust, three-dimensional situations that are concept-laden. This becomes particularly vivid in cases where expertise comes into play. Imagine walking through a field with a trained herpetologist. You both see a snake. Your sensory experience may be phenomenologically indistinguishable from hers – the same curves of the body, the same mottled pattern. Yet what is presented to each of you differs. To you, it is simply a snake. To her, it is an Agkistrodon contortrix. The difference is not in your visual apparatus per se but in the concepts at work within perception. Her grasp of the relevant distinctions generates a conceptually richer, even if phenomenologically identical, presentational state. And because intuitions are not phenomenologically robust, there is no need for any difference in how things look. This is why perceptual expertise can subtly transform experience without altering its sensory character.

Perception, then, is a perfect illustration of the broader point about intuitions. Because they lack any robust phenomenology, intuitions serve their function in plain view without our taking explicit notice of them.

The person who declines to get in the stranger’s car, or who flags the email as a phishing attempt, or who walks away from the deal – these individuals are not acting irrationally or on mere feeling. They are responding to a genuine presentational state: something is showing up as creepy, fraudulent or wrong. The situation is presenting itself as having a certain character, and that presentation carries epistemic weight – not because it is infallible, but because it is the same kind of state that grounds all of our most basic cognitive contact with the world.

This is precisely what philosophers mean when they talk about intuition. The difference between the person on the bridge who immediately senses that pushing the bystander is wrong, and the person who declines to get into a stranger’s car, is not a difference in kind. It is a difference in context and control. The philosopher’s thought experiment is a deliberately engineered situation designed to isolate and interrogate a single intuitive response. The everyday case is messier, embedded in a richer context, and rarely examined. But the underlying capacity, the presentational apprehension of how things are, is the same.

What has been missing in our theorising, until now, is simply the explicit recognition of this continuity. Philosophers have a well-developed account of why rational intuitions carry epistemic weight. They have been slower to claim that this account extends naturally to the intuitions we act on every day. Once we see this, ‘vibes’ and gut feelings are neither vindicated wholesale nor dismissed as mere noise. Instead, they are brought into the same framework that governs our most careful reasoning. The task of philosophy, then, is not to decide whether to trust intuition. It is to understand the role it already plays, from the thought experiment to the uneasy feeling about a stranger, in almost every act of understanding.
